body.text: CA（Certificate Authority，憑證機構）負責依照憑證政策驗證申請資訊、核發及簽署憑證。瀏覽器則負責驗證信任鏈、網域名稱、有效期限與其他適用條件。
CA 不需要取得網站伺服器的私鑰才能替它簽發憑證。
NIST 的 CA 定義也明確包括核發憑證及相關憑證管理職責。
回到 P3-Q121 → C. Certificate Authority。
User 是憑證使用者或申請者，不是預設簽發機構。Browser 通常是驗證憑證的一方；ISP 提供網路連線服務，除非另有 CA 身分，否則不因為是 ISP 就能簽署受信任憑證。
7. 進階補充：HTTPS 不只是加密
TLS 1.3 的常見憑證式連線，結合了 ECDHE 金鑰建立、憑證與簽章驗證、金鑰導出，以及 AEAD 對稱加密。
因此，一條真正受保護的連線通常需要同時考慮機密性（Confidentiality）、完整性（Integrity）及身分驗證（Authentication）。
只有加密而沒有適當的身分驗證，可能仍遭遇中間人攻擊；只有 Hash 而沒有受保護的驗證方式，也不能保證資料沒有遭到有意竄改。

sections.heading: 續篇供稿｜四、逐題判斷的關鍵陷阱

body.text: 供稿列出九筆參考答案；部分題目的教學描述須加上條件，原題全文仍待核對。以下四個限制值得記在筆記中。

rows: 在指定技術與攻擊能力下，復原不可行
加密金鑰愈長就必然愈安全
還要考慮區塊大小、運作模式與實作
非對稱加密可以單獨解決所有金鑰交換問題
需要適當的金鑰建立協定及對等方驗證
有 Hash 就能防止竄改
需要可信摘要來源，或使用 MAC、簽章等機制

body.text: 這四項差異非常重要，因為 CEH 題目可能測試的是一個概念的典型功能，但在研究或實務環境中，你必須進一步問：此功能成立的安全假設是什麼？

sections.heading: 續篇供稿｜五、主動回憶與間隔複習

body.text: 以下七個主動回憶問題保留供稿題號。先自行回答，再回查本部分的原理解說；原附件未附卡片翻面的答案。
EC-Q535
合法白帽測試最重要的條件是什麼？
SOC Tier 1 和 BCP 解決的是相同問題嗎？
Purge 與 Clear 的安全保證有何不同？
EC-Q284
為什麼 Blowfish 使用 448-bit 金鑰仍不代表適合長時間大量資料加密？
EC-Q032
非對稱密碼學如何與對稱式加密合作？
Hash、HMAC 與 CA 簽署的憑證分別能做什麼？
建議複習間隔
以今天 2026/11/10 為起點的示範排程
這些是實務上的起始間隔，不是所有人都適用的固定遺忘曲線公式。
調整規則是：答錯或無法自行解釋，隔天再測；答對但猶豫，維持較短間隔；能正確回答並應用於新情境，再逐步延長間隔。每次複習應混入其他 M01、M20 題目，而非只重做這九題。
間隔學習（Spacing）及提取練習（Retrieval Practice）有研究支持，但具體最佳排程仍依內容、學習者及保留期限而變化。

sections.heading: 續篇供稿｜六、理解檢核｜5 道新情境題

body.text: 本組先不提供正解。請獨立作答並保留判斷理由，之後再依實際答案檢視推理與待補強概念。
情境 1
一家醫院授權你測試兩個指定 API。你發現第三個由外包商管理的 API 可能有高風險漏洞，但不在合約範圍內。最適當的行動是什麼？
A. 立即測試，因為發現漏洞可以保護病人
B. 暫停對該 API 的主動測試，請求確認或擴充授權
C. 只要不用破壞性工具，就可以先測試
D. 請另一位研究員測試，就不算違反自己的授權
情境 2
醫院要建立風險評估方法、處理 SOC 警報，以及制定重大災難期間的診療作業計畫。哪一組配對最符合各項工作的目的？
A. ISO 27002／Tier 3／SLA
B. ISO 27005／Tier 1／BCP
C. ISO 27701／SOC Manager／NDA
D. ISO 27001／Incident Commander／AUP
情境 3
一台存有敏感病歷的 SSD 即將交給外部回收商。磁碟曾加密，但目前無法確認是否有未加密區域或外部金鑰副本。最佳做法是什麼？
A. 刪除所有檔案並清空垃圾桶
B. 只要執行金鑰刪除就必然達到 Purge
C. 確認加密涵蓋範圍與媒體特性，採合適清除方法並驗證留證
D. 直接交給回收商，因為 SSD 難以復原
情境 4
某系統使用 64-bit 區塊加密演算法，金鑰為 256 bits，且持續在同一金鑰下處理大量資料。最值得優先進一步評估的是什麼？
A. 256-bit 金鑰代表不存在任何加密風險
B. 所有安全問題都只能由暴力破解造成
C. 區塊長度、運作模式與資料量可能造成生日界限相關風險
D. 把金鑰增加到 448 bits 就能保證解決所有問題
情境 5
一家企業 API 會將資料及其 SHA-256 值傳送給客戶，但攻擊者有機會同時修改兩者。企業另外使用 HTTPS，但客戶端未正確驗證伺服器憑證。哪項改善最合適？
A. 將 SHA-256 改為 Base64
B. 正確驗證 TLS 伺服器身分，並依需求採用經驗證的完整性保護機制
C. 將 SHA-256 重複計算十次即可解決身分驗證問題
D. 只提高資料壓縮率，避免攻擊者辨認內容
這次課程要建立的核心能力，是從題目描述辨識出真正的安全目標、所使用的技術，以及安全保證成立的必要條件。能夠做到這三件事，就不只是記住九個答案，而是具備分析更多 CEH 題目的基礎。

en.title: Part 2 | M01 × M20: governance, sanitization, encryption and certificate trust

sections.heading: Build a security knowledge map

body.text: This is part 2 of the dated set: nine references spanning M01 foundations and M20 cryptography. Understand the security problem before selecting a technology, role or management system; recognizing English words is only the starting point.

items: Permission: valid authorization and testing boundaries.
Risk assessment: assessing information-security risk.
Laboratory-grade recovery: the recovery capability addressed by purge.
64-bit block: block size, not key length.
One-way function: hashing, not reversible encryption.
Issuing and signing certificates: the responsibility of a CA.

body.text: 1. Why does security need multiple technologies?

Imagine managing hospital security: doctors log into records, patients access information online and the hospital commissions regular vulnerability tests. The issues include authorization, risk, monitoring, continuity, sanitization, encryption and trust, rather than only whether an intrusion occurred. The source’s “seven hospital security questions” diagram did not include its detailed nodes in the supplied text; the supplied five-unit table below carries the available knowledge structure.

rows: What permits testing another party’s system?
How do we prevent issues, detect attacks and continue operating?
How does deletion differ from secure sanitization?
How do we protect data and establish keys securely?
Has data changed, and is the website identity trusted?

body.text: 2. Connect the protection goals through CIA

body.name: cia
body.caption: CIA: three information-security objectives
body.description: These are fundamental information-security objectives used by NIST. The three columns are parallel objectives, not sequential steps.

items.title: C · Confidentiality
items.body:
Confidentiality
People without permission must not see the data

items.title: I · Integrity
items.body:
Integrity
Data must remain correct and trustworthy

items.title: A · Availability
items.body:
Availability
Usable when needed

body.text: Confidentiality means patient B cannot freely inspect patient A’s record. Integrity protects a 5 mg dose from an unauthorized change to 50 mg. Availability lets an emergency doctor obtain necessary records when needed. Strong encryption alone does not prevent ransomware from interrupting service; the five units protect CIA from different directions.

sections.heading: Unit 1 | White hats and authorization

body.text: Reference EC-Q535, connected to M01-03 ethical hacking, authorization and rules of engagement.
1. A locksmith and a thief may use the same techniques

A homeowner hires a locksmith to test a lock. The locksmith opens it with tools and recommends replacement within the agreement. Someone else opens the same lock without consent and claims merely to demonstrate insecurity. Motive alone does not establish authorization; assess the technique together with permission, purpose and conduct.
2. Understand the terminology

rows: A person exploring, analyzing or operating systems, not necessarily a criminal
Tests within lawful authorization and applicable rules
Checks exploitable weaknesses within a controlled scope
A party with authority permits specified conduct
Systems, assets and activities included in testing

body.text: ROE are more than “you may test.” An agreement might permit only test.example.com, exclude the production database, limit work to Saturday 01:00–04:00, prohibit disruptive stress testing and require immediate reporting of serious vulnerabilities to a designated contact. These are concrete boundaries.
3. The four labels do not share one classification axis

rows: May lack malicious intent but also lack authorization
Relies mainly on others’ ready-made attack tools
Describes proficiency, not an authorization category

body.text: Hat labels are not an exhaustive, mutually exclusive legal classification. A script kiddie may attack unlawfully, and an authorized tester who deliberately exceeds scope gains no exemption by calling themselves a white hat.
4. EC-Q535: permission and legal boundaries

The supplied clues are A company hires a hacker to test its network security by simulating real-world attacks and The hacker has permission and operates within legal boundaries. Has permission identifies authorization; operates within identifies a limit; legal boundaries adds the legal constraint.

rows: The question is not about technical proficiency
Malicious unlawful intrusion is not described

body.text: The supplied answer is D. Look for authorization and legality rather than guessing a role from the tool used.
5. Variation: private reporting does not replace authorization

A researcher actively tests a website without consent and later reports privately. Lack of malicious intent alone does not establish white-hat authorization. Ask whether permission exists, whether a public disclosure policy allows the specific activity and whether legal limits were exceeded. These questions demonstrate the underlying principle.

sections.heading: Unit 2 | ISO, SOC and business continuity

body.text: References P1-Q063, P3-Q086 and P3-Q088 connect understanding risk, ongoing monitoring and triage, and maintaining critical business during disruption. They work together but concern different guidance, operational responsibilities and continuity planning.
1. Risk: start with an aging hospital server

A server still works, but its old software has publicly known vulnerabilities. Ask how important it is, how likely an attack is, how severe the consequences would be and how much protection to fund. These questions begin risk management.

rows: Medical database, server, account or healthcare service
Harm to an organization when a threat exploits a weakness

body.text: The attacker is a threat; an unpatched VPN flaw is a vulnerability. Exploiting it to access records is a risk scenario, while disclosure and service interruption are impacts. Threat and vulnerability are distinct.
2. Assess and treat risk
Teaching model: Risk ≈ Likelihood × Impact. Likelihood describes how probable the event is; impact describes its consequences. Suppose a hospital uses an illustrative 1–5 scale:

rows: Serious vulnerability in an external VPN

body.text: This is not an ISO-prescribed formula or rating. Organizations define their scales, tolerance and calculation or judgment method to support prioritization, not to turn risk into a magically precise number.

items: Risk mitigation: patch, strengthen authentication or restrict access.
Risk avoidance: stop a service whose risk cannot reasonably be controlled.
Risk sharing or transfer: share part of the loss through contracts or insurance.
Risk acceptance: an appropriately authorized party accepts residual risk.

body.text: Treatment does not automatically eliminate risk, and outsourcing a system does not necessarily remove the organization’s legal or management responsibilities.

rows: How do we establish policies, responsibilities, procedures, risk management and continual improvement?
How do we identify, analyze, assess and treat information-security risk?
Which specific controls can we use as guidance?
How do we manage responsibilities for collecting, using and processing patient personal data?

body.text: Both 27005 and 27002 support 27001; they are not a mandatory sequence in which one must be completed before using the other. ISMS means information security management system; PIMS means privacy information management system. The 2025 edition of 27701 replaces the 2019 edition.
4. P1-Q063: use the verbs to identify the standard’s task

Identify, assess, and treat information security risks as part of their ISMS identifies risk identification, assessment and treatment. The question asks for specialized guidance rather than overall ISMS requirements.

rows: Privacy management, not the most direct fit
Includes risk, but specifies overall system requirements
The most direct information-security risk guidance

body.text: The supplied answer is C. If the wording changes to ISMS requirements, choose 27001; risk guidance indicates 27005, while security-controls guidance indicates 27002.
5. SOC and initial triage

A security operations center, or SOC, resembles emergency-department triage: the first line assesses urgency and routes cases needing deeper work to appropriate specialists. Senior experts cannot deeply investigate every failed-login, suspicious-connection or malware alert.

Monitoring means continuously observing activity, such as repeated administrator-login attempts. Triage assesses an alert’s importance, credibility and need for escalation. It neither proves an attack completely nor requires Tier 1 to handle every vulnerability alone.

items: False positive: an alert is confirmed not to match the suspected malicious event.
False negative: malicious activity is present but not detected.
Escalation: route a case to personnel with deeper investigative capability or appropriate authority.

body.text: An employee traveling abroad and using an approved VPN may trigger an unfamiliar-location alert without an attack. Suspicious privilege escalation, data exports and endpoint activity accompanying that login strengthen the case for investigation.
6. Other SOC roles and threat hunting

rows: Investigate, analyze incidents and assist containment
Processes, staffing, performance and escalation procedures
Coordinate major response decisions and teams

body.text: Threat hunting proactively forms hypotheses and searches for attack traces not caught by existing alerts, whereas ordinary monitoring is more like responding when an alert fires. These are typical responsibilities, not a universal organization chart. Microsoft’s SOC guidance likewise distinguishes triage, investigation and advanced threat work.

Initial monitoring and triaging of security alerts points to first-line observation and classification. The supplied answer is A, Tier 1 Analyst. B, advanced analysis; C, management; and D, major-incident command are different responsibilities. Seeing SOC alone does not justify choosing manager.
8. BCP, DRP, IRP and recovery objectives

Ransomware blocks hospital records. The team investigates, isolates and restores systems, but emergency patients have already arrived. Care operations cannot simply wait for computer repair. A business continuity plan, or BCP, addresses maintaining or resuming necessary business when systems, facilities, personnel or supply chains are disrupted.
A BCP is broader than computer repair. It may include preapproved and rehearsed alternative care workflows, emergency communications, manual records, alternative work sites and resource coordination.

rows: How does the organization continue critical services?
How are information systems and data restored?
How is the incident investigated, contained and handled?

body.text: The three plans can operate together. RTO, recovery time objective, specifies the target time to restore the required condition after interruption. RPO, recovery point objective, specifies how far back in data state recovery from copies may be tolerated.

An RTO of 2 hours targets restoring the specified system within two hours. An RPO of 15 minutes targets avoiding a rollback to a data state more than 15 minutes before the incident. Written objectives are not guarantees; backups, technical capability and exercises must support them.

Which document outlines how a business will continue to operate during and after a significant disaster? Business, continue to operate, during and after, and significant disaster point to continuity during and following disruption. The supplied answer is C, BCP.

rows: Rules for acceptable equipment or service use

body.text: ISO 22301 addresses business continuity management systems. Service levels, confidentiality commitments and usage policies are not substitutes for a business continuity plan.
10. Recall the responsibilities with three hospital questions

items: Which risks should we address first? → ISO/IEC 27005.
Who initially triages a new alert? → SOC Tier 1.
How do essential services continue during disaster? → BCP.

body.text: The same reasoning about responsibilities transfers to a school, company or financial institution.

sections.heading: Unit 3 | Deletion, purge and sanitization

body.text: Reference P3-Q110. Distinguish deletion, data recovery and media sanitization.
1. Understand deletion through a library catalog

Removing a book from a library catalog may hide it from searches while leaving it on the shelf. File deletion can similarly remove a file or reference without securely sanitizing all underlying data. Filesystems, devices, TRIM and encryption affect the result; deletion neither guarantees nor rules out recovery.
2. Why can data recovery also be a risk?

Data recovery attempts to retrieve information after accidental deletion, filesystem damage or device failure using residual content, filesystem information, backups or other copies. It helps users but creates a risk when retiring sensitive equipment. A hospital selling an old computer that held test reports cannot treat file deletion alone as satisfying sanitization requirements.
3. Clear, purge and destroy
NIST SP 800-88 Rev. 2, published in September 2025, distinguishes three media-sanitization methods.

rows: Prevent simple, noninvasive recovery through normal user interfaces
Make recovery of target data infeasible with advanced laboratory techniques while potentially preserving reuse
Sanitize contents with a higher assurance objective
Make advanced recovery infeasible and prevent the medium from storing data again

body.text: 4. Why is purge not simply smashing a drive?

Purge classifies methods and assurance objectives, not one fixed action. Suitable device-sanitization functions or reliable cryptographic erase may achieve it. If data was properly encrypted, securely eliminating all required decryption keys can remove a feasible recovery path, like removing every usable key to reliably protected contents.

items: Since the last suitable sanitization, sensitive data has been suitably encrypted without residual plaintext writes.
The cryptography and key management are reliable.
No usable key copies remain.
Unencrypted regions have not been overlooked.
The method suits the device and security requirements.

body.text: Without these conditions, pressing “delete key” does not establish successful purge.
5. Retiring a hospital SSD: device characteristics matter

Before an SSD that held medical records goes to a recycler, select a method based on sensitivity, device capabilities and intended disposition, then verify the result and retain a record. This procedural explanation is an editorial addition based on sanitization principles; the original flowchart details were not supplied in the text.

Wear leveling distributes flash writes to extend lifetime. A logical address seen by the operating system does not necessarily keep mapping to the same physical area. Ordinary file-overwriting tools therefore cannot be assumed to sanitize all original SSD data.
What is the primary purpose of a "Purge" in the data destruction process? This asks for the sanitization objective rather than subsequent hardware disposition.

rows: A. To simply delete the file pointers.
Removing references is not sufficient assurance of sanitization
B. To make data recovery impossible even with laboratory-grade tools.
Best matches purge; interpret impossible as infeasible under the specified conditions
Recycling is a possible subsequent action, not the definition
D. To archive data for 10 years.
Archiving preserves information rather than sanitizing it

body.text: The supplied answer is B. Infeasible is not an unconditional mathematical impossibility.
7. Transfer the distinction to a new scenario

If confidential data must resist advanced recovery while equipment remains available for reuse by another department, consider purge. If the requirement is actual destruction and no further use as storage, it corresponds to destroy.

sections.heading: Unit 4 | Encryption, blocks, keys and distribution

body.text: References EC-Q284 and EC-Q032 connect symmetric and asymmetric cryptography. Ask what encryption and keys are, how data is processed, and how two parties obtain a shared secret.
1. Why encrypt? The algorithm and key have different roles

Hospital A sends a test report to hospital B, which should understand it while unauthorized third parties should not. Encryption transforms plaintext into ciphertext, and decryption uses the appropriate key and related information to recover it. A simplified symmetric path is plaintext plus encryption and a secret key → ciphertext → decryption with corresponding secret material → plaintext. Real schemes also involve IVs, nonces, modes and authentication tags.

rows: Recover data using suitable keys and related information

body.text: The algorithm resembles the design of a lock; a key is the particular secret setting controlling it. Modern cryptography should remain difficult to break when an attacker knows the algorithm but lacks the necessary secret. Publishing an algorithm does not make it insecure.
2. Symmetric encryption and key distribution

Symmetric encryption uses a shared secret key or corresponding secret material. It resembles encrypting with a common password that a colleague also uses to decrypt. It is usually efficient for databases, storage and large network transfers. But parties without an existing shared secret cannot safely send a key over an unprotected channel; that is the key-distribution problem.
3. Bit, byte, block and key size

A bit is 0 or 1; a byte is normally 8 bits. Thus 64 bits = 8 bytes and 128 bits = 16 bytes. A block is a fixed data unit transformed by a block cipher, while block size measures that unit in bits. Key size measures key length, a separate quantity.

An algorithm transforming 8 bytes at a time has a 64-bit block. An 8,000-byte file requires a suitable mode to process units and handle the final portion; the entire file is not limited to one block. Blowfish retains a 64-bit block regardless of its 32–448-bit key choice, while AES uses 128-bit blocks.
As an analogy, block size is the amount a machine processes at once, while key size relates to the number of possible secret settings. Both matter; the analogy only distinguishes their roles.
4. Block cipher and stream cipher

Block ciphers transform fixed-length blocks, as AES, Blowfish and Twofish do. Stream ciphers process data using mechanisms such as a keystream; RC4 and ChaCha20 are examples. An explicit 64-bit blocks clue calls for a matching block cipher rather than a stream cipher.
5. Specifications of four algorithms

Bruce Schneier introduced Blowfish in 1993; its design page documents 64-bit blocks and 32–448-bit keys. Twofish uses 128-bit blocks. NIST FIPS 197 specifies three AES key lengths, all with the same 128-bit block size.
6. EC-Q284: find the most discriminating clues

The financial company, disclosure, intercepted ciphertext and secure storage are background. The decisive clues are processes data in 64-bit blocks and supports a variable key size from 32 to 448 bits.

items: RC4 is a stream cipher; exclude it.
Twofish uses 128-bit blocks; exclude it.
AES has 128-bit blocks and not a 32–448-bit key range; exclude it.
Blowfish matches both clues; the supplied answer is D.

body.text: Being a DES alternative is plausible historical context, not a unique identifier. Actual ciphertext alone usually does not reveal the algorithm automatically; protocol negotiation, configuration or file-format evidence may be needed.
7. A longer key does not guarantee a safer system

A uniformly random 128-bit key has 2^128 possibilities. Each extra bit doubles the search space for brute force. Security also depends on blocks, modes, mathematical weaknesses, key generation and implementation, so comparing Blowfish 448 with AES 256 alone is insufficient.
8. The birthday bound and 64-bit blocks

Although there are 365 possible birthdays, 23 people already give approximately a greater-than-50% chance of a shared birthday. This birthday paradox illustrates why collisions matter. Under some modes, processing around 2^32 64-bit blocks with one key demands particular care.

At 8 bytes per block, 2^32 × 8 bytes = 34,359,738,368 bytes, approximately 34.4 GB or 32 GiB. Crossing that amount does not guarantee immediate disclosure; modes, key use and other attack conditions matter. Sweet32 in 2016 demonstrated attacks under particular TLS/OpenVPN and CBC conditions, not a universal fixed safe volume for all encryption.

A mode of operation specifies how to use a block cipher for longer messages; examples include CBC, CTR and GCM. AEAD, authenticated encryption with associated data, combines confidentiality with integrity and authentication of associated data when used correctly. AES is the core cipher; AES-GCM is a scheme using a particular mode. A long Blowfish key does not remove its small-block limitations.
9. Public/private keys, ECDHE and KDFs

Asymmetric cryptography uses mathematically related public and private keys. The public key can be shared; the private key must be protected. In a public-key encryption scheme, Alice can encrypt using Bob’s trusted public key and Bob can decrypt with his private key. Not every asymmetric algorithm encrypts documents, and this does not imply directly processing large files that way.

ECDHE, ephemeral elliptic-curve Diffie–Hellman, lets both parties exchange public information and locally compute a shared secret without transmitting that secret directly. This is key agreement. A key derivation function, or KDF, derives session keys, which symmetric mechanisms use to protect bulk data.

A common hybrid division is public-key mechanisms establish secret material → a KDF derives keys → symmetric mechanisms protect data. Symmetric cryptography is generally better suited to bulk data, while public-key mechanisms handle key establishment and signatures rather than directly encrypting everything.
10. EC-Q032: key distribution
Which encryption method supports secure key distribution? Identify the category that best supports establishing keys securely.

rows: A storage-protection use case rather than the typical initial key-distribution principle
Needs an existing shared secret; it can protect other keys, such as through key wrapping, under existing management, but is not the most direct answer here
A digest alone does not establish a secure shared secret
The best match among the four options

body.text: The supplied answer is D. A real design must specify the actual protocol and authentication. Establishing a secret does not identify the peer: a man in the middle can replace public values and establish separate secrets with the two endpoints. Key establishment therefore needs trusted authentication, leading to PKI and CAs.

sections.heading: Unit 5 | Hashes, signatures, PKI and CAs

body.text: References P3-Q074 and P3-Q121 distinguish checking whether content changed from checking whether its source is genuine. The two questions require different evidence.
1. Hash: a fixed-length digital fingerprint

Hashing resembles a machine calculating a fixed-length fingerprint from document content. The hash function produces a hash value, digest or message digest. SHA-256 outputs 256 bits for a short text or any file size within its permitted input range.

body.name: hash
body.caption: Different content usually produces different hashes
body.description: The two inputs are compared in parallel. Digest A/B are conceptual labels, not computed SHA-256 results. Collisions exist mathematically; security requires that exploitable collisions be difficult to find.

items.title: Input A
items.body:
Patient blood pressure: 120
↓ SHA-256
Produces digest A

items.title: Input B
items.body:
Patient blood pressure: 180
↓ SHA-256
Produces digest B, usually different from A

body.text: Changing one character usually changes the output substantially, but hashes are not unique for every possible input. More possible inputs than fixed-length outputs means collisions must exist. Secure hashing requires that exploitable collisions be difficult to find, along with properties such as one-way behavior.
2. One-way does not mean inputs cannot be guessed

A one-way function is easy to compute from input to digest but difficult to invert from digest to original. Encryption has a decryption procedure for appropriate key holders; hashing is not designed to decrypt a digest.

body.name: compare
body.caption: Encryption and hashing have different directions
body.description: Encryption has a corresponding decryption procedure; hashing has no decryption operation. Low-entropy inputs can still be guessed and hashed for comparison. That is guessing an input, not decrypting a digest.

items.title: Encryption
items.body:
Plaintext
↓ Algorithm and key
Ciphertext
↑ The appropriate key can recover the plaintext

items.title: Hashing
items.body:
Original data
↓ Hash function
Digest
No corresponding decryption operation

body.text: If a password comes from a small set such as 1234 or 0000, an attacker can hash candidates and compare them. That is guessing the input, not reverse decryption.
3. Conditions for checking changes with a hash

A hospital provides a report’s SHA-256 through a trusted channel. Recalculate it after receiving the file. A mismatch indicates different data or computation conditions; a match provides strong consistency evidence under the security assumptions and trusted-reference condition. Hashing does not prevent modification. If an attacker replaces both the document and the posted digest, comparison alone may miss the attack.
4. HMAC: authentication using a shared secret

HMAC, hash-based message authentication code, combines a hash with a shared secret key. Anyone can compute an ordinary hash; generating a valid HMAC requires secret material. Hospital A calculates it with a shared key and hospital B verifies with that key. An attacker lacking the key cannot simply change the data and recompute an ordinary hash to produce a valid HMAC.

NIST FIPS 198-1 describes this definition; its website also notes a plan to move the content to SP 800-224. Both holders of the shared key can generate HMACs, so an HMAC alone does not identify which holder sent a message. This differs from a publicly verifiable signature.
5. Digital signature: private-key signing and public-key verification

A digital signature provides integrity and evidence associated with the private key corresponding to a public key. Conceptually, data undergoes the scheme’s hashing/encoding and private-key signing, then travels with the signature. A receiver verifies using the trusted public key and specified scheme. Details depend on the algorithm; signing is not generically encrypting a hash with a private key.

rows: Encrypt with the recipient’s public key; decrypt with the recipient’s private key
Sign with the signer’s private key; verify with the corresponding public key

body.text: If the public key’s identity is unknown, mathematical verification does not establish the real-world signer. Key and identity management remain necessary.
6. P3-Q074 and encoding
Which of the following is a "one-way" function used to ensure data integrity? One-way, function and data integrity indicate hashing.

rows: Has encryption/decryption, not the requested one-way digest
Public-key encryption, not this digest function
A representation, not equivalent to cryptographic hashing or encryption

body.text: The supplied answer is C. Base64 represents binary data as text for transmission or storage. Anyone can decode it using public rules; it does not provide confidentiality.
7. PKI: possessing a public key is insufficient

An attacker can generate a key pair and claim, just as a bank does, “This is my public key.” A system is needed to bind keys to identities or domains through trusted processes. PKI, public key infrastructure, includes certificates, CAs, trust anchors and management/validation procedures.
8. CA: the certificate issuer

A CA, certificate authority, resembles a credential issuer. A company applies for a website certificate; the CA validates information under its policy and issues it. The certificate includes the public key, applicable identity information, validity, issuer and signature. The CA signature lets a browser validate the issuing chain under its trust policy.
9. Certificate chain: from root to website

rows: An intermediate authorized by an issuer above it
Website public key and domain-related information

body.text: Browsers or operating systems maintain trusted root sets in common Web PKI, and actual chains vary in depth. Validation checks more than a CA signature: chain, name, validity, purpose and constraints matter. A publicly trusted certificate does not guarantee lawful business conduct, safe content or absence of malware. Its trust concerns the specified identity/key relationship.
10. How does HTTPS combine the mechanisms?

HTTPS is HTTP protected by TLS. Common certificate-based TLS 1.3 combines asymmetric key establishment such as ECDHE, CA certificates and server authentication, key derivation and symmetric AEAD such as AES-GCM. The following preserves endpoints, message directions and local validation responsibilities.

body.name: tls
body.caption: TLS 1.3: simplified certificate-based ECDHE exchange
body.description: Solid arrows mean browser-to-server messages; dashed arrows mean server replies, not unencrypted traffic. Orange boxes indicate local computation or validation. EncryptedExtensions, key-schedule details, client certificates and other branches are omitted; this is not a packet capture. Server handshake messages from Certificate onward are protected with handshake keys.

items.title: ClientHello + key_share
items.body: The browser offers supported parameters and a public key share.

items.title: ServerHello + key_share
items.body: The server selects parameters and returns its public key share.

items.title: Compute a shared secret and derive keys locally
items.body: ECDHE and HKDF establish handshake keys. The key schedule later derives application traffic keys; the shared secret is not sent directly.

items.title: Certificate
items.body: The server sends its certificate chain, carrying public-key and identity/domain binding information.

items.title: CertificateVerify
items.body: A signature proves possession of the corresponding private key and binds the handshake transcript.

items.title: Finished (server)
items.body: A verification value based on handshake secrets and the transcript authenticates this handshake.

items.title: Validate certificate, domain, signature and Finished
items.body: The browser checks the trust chain, name, validity and applicable constraints. Failure prevents continuing a trusted connection. This box groups validation responsibilities rather than prescribing exact execution timing.

items.title: Finished (browser)
items.body: The browser sends its handshake confirmation; client-certificate authentication is omitted in this example.

items.title: Encrypted HTTP request
items.body: Application traffic keys and an AEAD such as AES-GCM protect the request.

items.title: Encrypted HTTP response
items.body: The server protects its reply with traffic keys for its direction. The CA does not participate in every handshake.

body.text: RFC 9846 replaced RFC 8446 in 2026 as the TLS 1.3 specification; it remains version 1.3. The diagram omits messages and details and is not a packet capture. A CA need not participate in each connection or possess a website’s private key. The server proves possession during the handshake and the client validates the certificate and peer.
11. P3-Q121: issuance and validation are different jobs
In a "Public Key Infrastructure" (PKI), who is responsible for issuing and signing digital certificates? Issuing and signing are different from validating a certificate during a connection.

rows: An applicant or user, not the default issuer
Issues and signs certificates; the supplied answer
Being an ISP does not automatically make an entity a CA

body.text: The supplied answer is C. If asked who validates a server certificate during HTTPS, think browser or another TLS client. Matching the action to its responsible role is more reliable than memorizing the reference number.

body.text: 1. Use four steps for every question

items: For P3-Q121, first identify the real question: who issues and signs certificates?
Find the clue Issuing and Signing Digital Certificates.
Recall that the CA issues certificates.
Exclude browser (validator), user (consumer) and ISP (not automatically a CA), giving C.

body.text: Reasoning that survives changed reference numbers and option order is more reliable than memorizing “P3-Q121 = C.”
2. Review the nine references

items: 27001 versus 27005: system requirements versus risk-management guidance.
Clear, purge and destroy: different recovery-resistance objectives and media outcomes.
Block size versus key size: data-unit length versus secret-material length.
Hash, HMAC, signature and CA: digests, shared-secret authentication, private-key signing and certificate trust have different roles.

sections.heading: Eight active-recall cards

body.text: Recall the principle before revealing the answer. The eight prompts are supplied; reference answers are editorial additions derived from the body.

body.caption: Eight active-recall cards
body.description: Answer before revealing explanations. Viewing an answer does not establish learning; this page does not record personal progress.

cards.question: Is attack-tool ability the main difference between white and black hats?
answer: No. The same tools can be used with different authorization, purpose and conduct. First check valid permission and boundaries.

cards.question: How do ISO/IEC 27001, 27002 and 27005 differ?
answer: 27001 specifies ISMS requirements, 27002 gives control guidance and 27005 gives risk-management guidance. The latter two support the first, without a fixed mandatory sequence.

cards.question: Who initially triages an alert, and which plan supports service during a hospital disaster?
answer: Typically Tier 1 monitors and triages initially. A BCP maintains essential business and works with the DRP and IRP.

cards.question: Why is ordinary deletion not automatically purge?
answer: Deletion may remove only references. Purge needs a suitable device-specific method and verification that advanced laboratory recovery of target data is infeasible.

cards.question: What do Blowfish’s 64-bit and 448-bit values describe?
answer: 64 bits is block size; 448 bits is the supported maximum key length. Increasing the key does not enlarge the block.

cards.question: Why does modern TLS often combine asymmetric and symmetric cryptography?
answer: A certificate-based ECDHE connection uses public-key mechanisms for secret establishment and authentication, a KDF for keys, and symmetric AEAD for bulk data. Correct peer validation is still required.

cards.question: Why can an ordinary SHA-256 digest not alone prove absence of malicious modification?
answer: If an attacker replaces both data and digest, comparison can still match. Use a trusted reference digest or suitable authentication such as a MAC or signature.

cards.question: How do a CA and browser differ in PKI?
answer: A CA validates applications under policy and issues certificates. A browser validates the chain, name, validity and related conditions under its connection trust policy.

sections.heading: Five final understanding checks

body.text: These five supplied scenario exercises are not copies of official questions. Answer independently. The source did not supply explanations; the following option analyses are editorial references based on the body, not teacher grading or official exam scoring.

items.prompt: A team testing a hospital’s production website discovers a potentially serious flaw in an internal system absent from the authorization list. What should it do?
options: A. Test every hospital system because the hospital authorized testing
B. Confirm scope and obtain expanded authorization when needed
C. Test freely as long as no damage occurs
D. Assume legality if findings are kept private
rationales: Permission for specified targets does not cover every system.
Confirming and changing authorization respects scope.
Avoiding damage does not grant permission.
Private reporting does not replace authorization and legal limits.

items.prompt: A hospital needs risk-management guidance, initial alert triage and a disaster continuity plan. Which sequence fits best?
options: A. ISO 27005, Tier 1, BCP
B. ISO 27002, Tier 3, NDA
C. ISO 27701, SOC Manager, SLA
D. ISO 27001, Incident Commander, AUP
rationales: These match risk guidance, first-line triage and continuity.
Control guidance, advanced analysis and confidentiality agreements do not match the requested tasks.
Privacy standards, management and service agreements do not match all three responsibilities.
Overall system requirements, incident command and use policies are not the most direct combination.

items.prompt: A customer-data SSD will be reused by another department, with advanced laboratory recovery required to be infeasible. What fits best?
options: A. Ordinary file deletion
B. Empty the recycle bin
C. Select and verify a purge method suitable for the SSD
D. Rename the partition
rationales: Ordinary deletion does not provide that assurance.
Emptying a bin is not suitable sanitization.
This matches recovery resistance and potential reuse.
Renaming does not sanitize underlying data.

items.prompt: Does selecting the longest key eliminate bulk-encryption risk for a cipher with 64-bit blocks and keys up to 448 bits?
options: A. It is AES and its key is long enough
B. It may be Blowfish, but blocks, mode and use conditions still matter
C. It must be RC4 because its key length varies
D. A 448-bit key eliminates collision and implementation risk
rationales: AES does not have a 64-bit block.
A longer key does not remove small-block or usage limitations.
RC4 is not a fixed 64-bit block cipher.
Key length does not eliminate other risks.

items.prompt: Which statement correctly relates trusted HTTPS certificates, protected transport and a download’s trusted publisher?
options: A. SHA-256 alone performs all validation
B. The CA encrypts every website packet
C. Correct TLS certificate validation and AEAD protect the connection; publisher trust may also require a signature or another trusted release mechanism
D. Base64 replaces TLS and PKI
rationales: An unprotected digest does not authenticate the source and connection.
The CA signs certificates, not every connection’s data packets.
This distinguishes connection protection from publisher evidence.
Encoding does not supply these security functions.

A protective security system must address who may act, how risk is managed, how incidents are handled, how data is protected and why another party can be trusted. Installing tools and encrypting data alone does not establish all of these protections.
This batch contains nine references, questions 10–18, covering seven curriculum subsections. They are integrated into five knowledge units to avoid repeatedly teaching the same idea.

Understand ISO risk-management standards, SOC tiers and business continuity planning.

Explain symmetric and asymmetric cryptography and distinguish block size from key size.
Explain how hashes, HMAC, digital signatures, CAs, PKI and TLS support information security together.

body.text: Supplied answer overview

rows: A CA issues and signs certificates

body.text: The source author reports reconsidering the answers using the prompts and technical standards. They remain supplied proposed answers; complete original questions and all options still require independent verification. Distinguish the following four exam simplifications from operational facts:

items: Purge in question 11 does not mathematically guarantee that recovery is absolutely impossible; it makes recovery using state-of-the-art laboratory techniques infeasible.
ISO/IEC 27005 in question 12 provides risk-management guidance; ISO/IEC 27001 specifies ISMS requirements.
Asymmetric cryptography in question 16 can establish shared keys, but asymmetric encryption alone does not universally prevent man-in-the-middle attacks.
A hash in question 17 can reveal differences, but without a trusted reference or verification mechanism it cannot alone resist malicious modification.

sections.heading: Continuation | 2. The overall knowledge map

body.text: Consider a hospital that provides online access to patient records.
It must protect personal data, authorize security testing, monitor attacks, maintain services and prevent record disclosure when equipment is retired.
This integrated teaching model does not mean that ISO standards require every measure to follow this single sequence.

rows: How are protections selected, alerts handled and operations maintained?
How is unwanted data securely sanitized?
How is confidentiality protected and key material established?
How do we assess modification and the other party's identity?

body.text: The following units develop these five topics.

sections.heading: Continuation | 3. Integrated core concepts

body.text: Unit 1 | When is a hacker providing authorized assistance? (question 10)
1. Plain-language explanation: a locksmith tests your lock
You ask a locksmith to open your door to assess whether the lock is secure.
Opening it reveals a weakness. With your valid authorization and compliance with the agreed test, the locksmith is conducting an authorized security check.
If the same locksmith tests a neighbor's lock without consent, intending to report a problem does not automatically make the activity lawful.
Authorization, scope and conduct provide the relevant distinction; technical capability alone does not.
2. Formal definition
A white-hat hacker is an authorized security researcher or tester working to improve security.
Organizational testing usually involves two important documents or agreements:

items: Authorization: formal permission to conduct the work.
Rules of engagement (ROE): the permitted targets, time, techniques, restrictions and response procedures.

body.text: 3. How it works: authorized testing has boundaries

body.name: authorization
body.caption: Four steps in authorized testing
body.description: Arrows show work dependencies. The authorizer must represent the target assets; scope and ROE constrain testing.

items.title: Obtain testing authorization
items.body: Confirm who has authority over the target assets

items.title: Agree scope and ROE
items.body: Targets, time, methods, data handling and stopping conditions

items.title: Test and preserve evidence
items.body: Limit impact and avoid unnecessary data collection

items.title: Report vulnerabilities and remediation
items.body: Enable the organization to reduce actual risk

body.text: 4. Practical example
A hospital hires a team to test patient.example.com. The contract authorizes only that website and specified test APIs.
The testers discover another hospital system operated by a contractor. A shared brand or domain does not establish that this system is covered by the authorization.
OWASP testing guidance also emphasizes scope, authorization, safe-harbor conditions and ROE.
5. Compare the categories

rows: Authorized testing for defense and security improvement
May lack authorization without necessarily intending malicious damage
Reliance on ready-made tools with limited technical understanding; not a legal authorization category

body.text: 6. Return to EC-Q535
The supplied answer is D. White Hat Hacker.

The decisive conditions are engagement by the organization, permission and compliance with legal boundaries. A is unsuitable because Script Kiddie describes capability and behavior; B and C do not fit the stated authorization scenario.
7. Further considerations
Authorization does not permit every action. Accidentally obtaining real patient records still requires data minimization, confidentiality and notification procedures.
White-hat professionalism includes controlling testing risk and protecting the organization as well as finding vulnerabilities.
Unit 2 | How do risk management, the SOC and BCP work together? (questions 12–14)
These three questions address different responsibilities:
How are risks managed before an incident? How are problems detected during operations? How do essential operations continue during a disaster?
1. Plain-language explanation: imagine a hospital as a ship
Before sailing, the captain assesses weather and equipment risks: risk management.
During the voyage, someone watches the radar and reports anomalies: a role analogous to the SOC.
If the engine fails, backup power, communications and emergency navigation plans keep the ship functioning: an analogy for BCP.
These functions cannot replace one another.
2. Formal definitions: the ISO 27000 family

rows: Identify controls that may be selected

body.text: 27001 and 27005 are particularly easy to confuse.
ISO/IEC 27001 sets management requirements for an ISMS; ISO/IEC 27005 provides focused guidance on activities such as information-security risk assessment and treatment.
Version check: option A in question 12 names ISO/IEC 27701:2019, replaced in 2025 by ISO/IEC 27701:2025. This does not change the intended answer.
3. How it works: from risk to business continuity
Suppose the hospital uses a VPN appliance for an externally accessible login service.

rows: Patient-record service interruption and data disclosure
Patch, restrict access, improve monitoring and maintain backups

body.text: Risk assessment involves threats, vulnerabilities, likelihood, business impact and existing controls; calculating a CVSS score alone is insufficient.
Common treatment strategies include mitigation, avoidance, sharing or transferring some losses, and acceptance. Acceptance still requires a decision by the appropriate risk owner.
What happens if attacks continue despite the protections?
The security operations center (SOC) provides monitoring and response functions.

body.name: soc
body.caption: A common SOC triage workflow
body.description: No leads to recording, closure or observation; yes leads to Tier 2 and optionally Tier 3. Either investigation tier can activate major-incident command. Automation or MDR may perform these roles.

items.title: SIEM / EDR alert
items.body: Enter incident triage

items.title: Tier 1 initial confirmation and classification
items.body: Check the alert and escalation criteria

items.title: Enough evidence for further investigation?
items.body: Choose the branch using evidence

items.title: Record, close or continue observing
items.body: Retain records and monitor when evidence is insufficient

items.title: Tier 2 investigation and response
items.body: Investigate evidence and support response

items.title: Escalate to Tier 3 when needed
items.body: Advanced analysis / threat hunting

items.title: Activate major-incident command
items.body: Coordinate response, decisions and communication

rows: Initial monitoring, alert confirmation, classification and escalation assessment
Detailed analysis, evidence investigation and incident handling or support
Complex analysis, threat hunting and detection improvements
Team, process, resource, quality and performance management
Coordination, decisions and communication during major incidents

body.text: Microsoft Defender operational guidance also assigns triage, prioritization and escalation when required to Tier 1.
4. Practical example: a ransomware attack on a hospital
At 2 a.m., EDR reports unusually large numbers of file operations on a server.

Tier 1 checks credibility, affected assets and escalation thresholds. Tier 2 investigates processes, network connections and affected devices. If a major incident is confirmed, the response team isolates, communicates and recovers according to established procedures.
Patients still need care now; they cannot simply wait for technical repairs.
A business continuity plan (BCP) may therefore activate approved alternative record procedures, adjust nonurgent services and maintain emergency communications until core systems recover.
5. Compare BCP, DRP and IRP

rows: How does the hospital keep treating patients during an outage?
How are databases, servers and networks restored?
Detecting, analyzing and handling security incidents
How is ransomware confirmed and contained?

body.text: BCP spans the business, while DRP usually focuses on technical recovery. ISO 22301 is a related international business-continuity management standard.
Two further objectives matter:

items: RTO: recovery time objective, the target time for restoring operations or service.
RPO: recovery point objective, the maximum tolerable period of lost data.

body.text: An RPO of 15 minutes does not prove that the system achieves it. Backups, replication and actual recovery-test results must also be checked.
6. Return to the three references

P1-Q063 → C. ISO/IEC 27005:2022. Identifying, assessing and treating information-security risk points to 27005. 27001 contains overall ISMS requirements, 27002 provides control guidance and 27701 addresses privacy information management.

P3-Q086 → A. Tier 1 Analyst. The key phrase is initial monitoring and triaging. Tier 3, the SOC Manager and the Incident Commander are not the default first-line triage roles in the described situation.

P3-Q088 → C. BCP. The question concerns continuing operations during and after a major disaster. An SLA is a service-level agreement, an NDA is a nondisclosure agreement and an AUP is an acceptable-use policy; none is a business continuity plan.
7. Further considerations: incident response and business continuity have distinct purposes
A mature organization addresses both questions:
“Can we stop the attack spreading?” and “Can the most important services continue before the attack is fully resolved?”

Focusing only on containment may leave the technical team with an isolated attack but no workable alternative process for clinical operations.
EOF
Unit 3 | How do Delete, Clear, Purge and Destroy differ? (question 11)
1. Plain-language explanation: is a discarded document really gone?
Imagine four approaches:
First, remove the directory record, like removing a book from a library catalog while leaving the book on its shelf.
Second, sanitize the data appropriately so ordinary interfaces cannot readily recover it.
Third, use stronger sanitization so recovery using advanced laboratory techniques is infeasible within the relevant effort level.
Fourth, physically destroy the medium holding the data.
The approaches provide different levels of assurance.
2. Formal definitions
NIST SP 800-88 Rev. 2, Guidelines for Media Sanitization, was finalized on September 26, 2025, superseding Rev. 1 from 2014. It is an important current reference for this topic.

rows: Remove a file or logical reference; not equivalent to sanitization
Prevent recovery through ordinary user interfaces
Make recovery of target data using advanced laboratory techniques infeasible
Physically render the medium unusable for data storage
Media that will not be reused or must be destroyed

body.text: 3. How it works: Purge concerns infeasible recovery
NIST's Purge definition concerns physical or logical techniques that make recovery of target data using state-of-the-art laboratory methods infeasible.
This does not mean one command is appropriate for every drive.

Hard disks, SSDs, USB drives and other media work differently. SSDs have a flash translation layer (FTL) and spare areas; overwriting user-visible sectors may leave other original data locations untouched.
Another important technique is cryptographic erase (CE).

If all relevant data was appropriately encrypted and all necessary decryption keys can be securely sanitized, CE may meet the sanitization objective. Whether it qualifies as Purge depends on the encryption implementation, key copies, media support and sanitization verification.
4. Practical example
A hospital plans to hand an SSD containing patient records to an external recycler.
Selecting “delete files” in the operating system does not establish that the records were securely sanitized.

Assess data sensitivity, media type, reuse plans and supported methods, then execute, verify and record the sanitization. If reliable sanitization is unavailable and reuse is unnecessary, suitable physical destruction may be required.
5. Compare the approaches
Purge and Destroy are distinct.
Purge generally aims to retain a reusable medium while making recovery of the old data infeasible; Destroy removes the medium's original storage utility.
The scope also extends beyond the primary drive. Snapshots, backups, other storage nodes and external backup copies require their own lifecycle management.
6. Return to P3-Q110
The supplied answer is B. To make data recovery impossible even with laboratory-grade tools.
“Impossible” is imprecise. The exam intends resistance to laboratory-grade recovery, while the standard uses the concept of infeasibility.
A only removes file pointers, C concerns hardware recycling rather than the sanitization definition and D concerns archiving, the opposite lifecycle direction from destruction.
7. Further considerations
An operational decision requires more than identifying the tool used:
“Does it actually work for this medium and data scope, and what verification evidence supports that conclusion?”
NIST Rev. 2 emphasizes organization-wide sanitization management, method applicability and trust in vendor implementations, rather than providing only a fixed set of disk-overwrite commands.
Unit 4 | Symmetric encryption and asymmetric cryptography (questions 15–16)
1. Plain-language explanation: locking data in a safe
Imagine sending a confidential report to a colleague.
You lock a safe with a key and your colleague opens it with the same key: an analogy for symmetric encryption.
A further problem remains:
How will you deliver the key securely?
If you send it over an insecure network, an attacker may steal the key before opening the safe.
Public-key cryptography helps address this kind of key-establishment problem.
2. Formal definitions

rows: A shared secret key or corresponding shared key material
Key establishment, signatures and some encryption uses
Usually better suited to large data volumes
Usually not used directly for bulk encryption
Distinct mechanisms such as RSA, ECDH/ECDHE and ECDSA
Authenticate public keys and protect private keys

body.text: ECDH/ECDHE are asymmetric key-agreement mechanisms, not conventional public-key encryption. ECDSA is a signature algorithm. Each is an application of public-key cryptography.
3. How it works: block size and key size are distinct
This is the central technical distinction in question 15.
Suppose a block cipher processes 64 bits, or 8 bytes, at a time.
Its block size is 64 bits.
Its encryption key may have a different length, called the key size.
Block size specifies the amount of data processed per block. Key size affects the key space and brute-force difficulty, while other factors also affect security.

body.name: blocksize
body.caption: Block size and key size are independent
body.description: Bar lengths use 128 bits as the reference. Blowfish supports 32–448-bit keys while retaining 64-bit blocks; a longer key does not enlarge the block.

items.title: Blowfish block
items.body: 64 bits = 8 bytes

items.title: AES block
items.body: 128 bits = 16 bytes

body.text: 4. Practical example: distinguish Blowfish, Twofish and AES

rows: Stream cipher; unsuitable for new systems

body.text: Bruce Schneier's original design documentation confirms Blowfish's properties. Twofish design documents and NIST FIPS 197 provide the corresponding Twofish and AES specifications.
A significant security issue follows.
A 256-bit Blowfish key may look long enough to imply complete security.
Its 64-bit blocks still introduce birthday-bound concerns. In certain modes and high-volume uses, collisions become important around a scale of 2^32 blocks.

Sweet32 demonstrates attacks on 64-bit block ciphers under particular long-lived connection and protocol conditions. Increasing a Blowfish key from 128 to 448 bits does not automatically eliminate that issue.
5. Compare the approaches: why are hybrid cryptographic systems common?
Typical modern HTTPS combines the strengths of several mechanisms rather than relying solely on symmetric or asymmetric cryptography.

body.name: hybrid
body.caption: Roles in hybrid cryptography
body.description: ECDHE and certificate/signature validation have distinct roles, converging on authenticated AEAD protection. This is a functional dependency diagram, not an exact TLS packet timeline.

items.title: Asymmetric establishment: ECDHE
items.body: Produce a shared secret

items.title: Shared secret
items.body: Input to key derivation

items.title: KDF derives connection keys
items.body: Do not use the raw secret directly for every purpose

items.title: Certificates / digital signatures
items.body: Provide authentication evidence

items.title: Authenticate the peer
items.body: Validate the peer and handshake trust relationship

items.title: Symmetric AEAD, such as AES-GCM
items.body: Protect data with correct nonces, keys and verification

items.title: Protected application data
items.body: Confidentiality and integrity protection

body.text: 6. Return to the two references
EC-Q284 → D. Blowfish.
The decisive combination is a 64-bit block and a variable 32–448-bit key. Twofish and AES use 128-bit blocks; RC4 is not a block cipher.
“Replacement for DES” is supporting evidence, not sufficient identification: several algorithms have been designed or evaluated as DES replacements.
In practice, a captured ciphertext segment alone usually cannot establish which algorithm produced it. Protocol information, implementation records or other evidence is also needed.
EC-Q032 → D. Asymmetric Encryption.
Among the four options, asymmetric cryptography best fits secure key distribution or establishment.
Disk encryption is a use case. Symmetric encryption presupposes handling the shared-key problem. Hash functions do not by themselves securely deliver a recoverable key to another party.
7. Further considerations
TLS 1.3 can establish a shared secret with ECDHE, derive traffic keys and use AEAD (authenticated encryption with associated data), such as AES-GCM, to protect data.

RFC 9846, published in July 2026, supersedes RFC 8446 as the updated TLS 1.3 specification. It retains the main architecture while tightening requirements, including forbidding reuse of KeyShare values between connections.
A secure cryptographic system depends on key management, authentication, modes and implementation details as well as algorithm names.
Unit 5 | Hashes, MACs, signatures and PKI (questions 17–18)
1. Plain-language explanation: document fingerprints and identity evidence
Imagine sending an important contract to a colleague.
You want to check two things:
First, has the contract changed?
Second, did it really come from you?
These are separate questions.
A hash helps compare content but does not alone establish the sender's identity.
Authenticating a source requires a mechanism such as a shared secret key or a digital signature.
2. Formal definitions

rows: Authenticate integrity and a shared-key holder
Authenticate the signer and data integrity
Establish a trusted binding between identity and public key
The CA uses a signing key
Manage public keys, certificates and trust relationships

body.text: 3. How it works: why is a hash called one-way?
Suppose SHA-256 receives this input:
hospital-record-001
It produces a 256-bit digest. Changing the original data normally changes the digest.

body.name: digest
body.caption: Hashes produce data digests
body.description: The rows are parallel comparisons: normally Hash(A) differs from Hash(B). Detecting malicious alteration needs a trusted reference; collisions between distinct inputs remain possible.

items.title: Original document A
items.body: Hash(A)

items.title: Modified document B
items.body: Hash(B)

body.text: Cryptographic hash functions seek these properties:

items: Preimage resistance: given a digest, finding an input that produces it is computationally difficult.
Second-preimage resistance: given one input, finding a different input with the same digest is difficult.
Collision resistance: finding any two different inputs with the same digest is difficult.

body.text: “One-way” means computationally difficult to reverse. It does not prevent dictionary guessing of short passwords or other low-entropy inputs.
4. Practical example: replacing both the file and its hash
You download a program from a website that also publishes its SHA-256 digest.
Your computed digest matches the published value.
Does that establish that the program is safe?
No.
An attacker who controls both the program and the website's digest can replace both.
Hashes support integrity checking, but resisting malicious replacement requires a trusted digest source or keyed authentication such as HMAC or a digital signature.
5. Compare Hash, HMAC and Signature

items: Hash: “Do these data values match?”
HMAC: “Was this data produced by a holder of the shared secret and left unmodified?”
Digital signature: “Was this data signed by the corresponding private-key holder and left unmodified?”

body.text: HMAC combines a cryptographic hash with a secret key. NIST defines it as a keyed message authentication code.
Because both parties share the secret, HMAC generally cannot independently establish which particular shared-key holder produced a message in the way a suitable digital-signature system can.
6. Return to P3-Q074
The supplied answer is C. Hashing.
The key phrase is one-way function.

Symmetric and asymmetric encryption primarily concern encryption that can be reversed using appropriate keys. Encoding transforms a data representation, such as Base64; it is not a cryptographic hash.
“Ensure data integrity” is abbreviated wording. A hash with a trusted comparison value supports integrity checking; an unprotected digest alone does not assure integrity against an active attacker.
PKI: who establishes that a public key belongs to the claimed party?
Suppose you open a bank website.
An attacker can generate their own public/private key pair and claim to be the bank.
A public key alone therefore does not establish a trusted identity.
Public key infrastructure (PKI) addresses this through certificates, certificate authorities and trust chains.

body.name: certificate
body.caption: Certificate-based TLS 1.3: CA, server and browser
body.description: The CA issues the certificate beforehand and need not participate in every handshake. Arrows indicate message direction; dashed replies do not denote encryption state. Optional messages and some encryption details are omitted; see RFC 9846.

items.title: Certificate authority (CA)
items.body: Validate the application and sign the certificate

items.title: Web server
items.body: Retain its own private key

items.title: Browser
items.body: Validate server identity

items.title: Complete certificate application and issuance beforehand
items.body: CA and server: before the connection

items.title: Issue and sign the certificate
items.body: CA → Web server

items.title: ClientHello + key_share
items.body: Browser → Web server

items.title: ServerHello + key_share
items.body: Web server → Browser

items.title: Certificate + CertificateVerify
items.body: Web server → Browser

items.title: Finished
items.body: Web server → Browser

items.title: Validate certificate chain, domain and signatures
items.body: Browser checks locally; this box groups validation duties

items.title: Finished
items.body: Browser → Web server

items.title: Protect application data with derived symmetric keys
items.body: Web server ↔ Browser

body.text: A certificate authority (CA) verifies application information under its certificate policy and issues and signs certificates. The browser validates the chain, domain name, validity period and other applicable conditions.
Issuing a website certificate does not require the CA to obtain the website server's private key.
NIST's CA definition also includes certificate issuance and associated certificate-management duties.
Return to P3-Q121 → C. Certificate Authority.

A user requests or uses a certificate rather than being its default issuer. A browser usually verifies certificates. An ISP supplies connectivity; being an ISP alone does not make it a trusted certificate-signing authority.
7. Further considerations: HTTPS combines several protections
A common certificate-based TLS 1.3 connection combines ECDHE key establishment, certificate and signature validation, key derivation and symmetric AEAD.
A protected connection therefore requires attention to confidentiality, integrity and authentication together.
Encryption without appropriate authentication may permit a man-in-the-middle attack. A hash without protected verification also does not establish resistance to intentional modification.

sections.heading: Continuation | 4. Important traps in interpreting the questions

body.text: The source supplies nine proposed answers. Some explanations need conditions, and the complete original questions still require verification. Record the following four limits.

rows: Recovery is infeasible under specified techniques and capabilities
A longer encryption key always means greater security
Also consider block size, mode and implementation
Asymmetric encryption alone solves every key-exchange problem
Use an appropriate establishment protocol and authenticate the peer
Use a trusted digest source or mechanisms such as MACs or signatures

body.text: CEH questions may ask about a mechanism's typical function. Research and operational decisions must also examine the security assumptions under which that function holds.

sections.heading: Continuation | 5. Active recall and spaced review

body.text: The seven recall prompts retain the supplied references. Answer first, then consult the explanations in this part; the attachment did not include the reverse-side answers.
EC-Q535
What are the essential conditions for an authorized white-hat test?
What do ISO/IEC 27001, 27002 and 27005 each address?
Do SOC Tier 1 and BCP solve the same problem?
How does Purge assurance differ from Clear?
EC-Q284
Why does a 448-bit Blowfish key not make it suitable for unlimited long-lived bulk encryption?
EC-Q032
How does asymmetric cryptography work with symmetric encryption?
What do hashes, HMAC and CA-signed certificates each establish?
Suggested review intervals
An example schedule starting on November 10, 2026
These are starting intervals for practical use, not a fixed forgetting-curve formula for everyone.

If an answer is wrong or cannot be explained, retest the next day. If correct but uncertain, retain a short interval. If correct reasoning transfers to a new scenario, gradually lengthen the interval. Mix other M01 and M20 questions into each review rather than repeating only these nine.
Research supports spacing and retrieval practice, while the best schedule depends on the material, learner and retention horizon.

sections.heading: Continuation | 6. Understanding check | five new scenarios

body.text: This set withholds answers. Attempt it independently and retain your reasoning for later review of your actual responses and conceptual gaps.
Scenario 1
A hospital authorizes testing of two specified APIs. You discover a potentially high-risk vulnerability in a third, contractor-managed API outside the contract. What is the most appropriate action?
A. Test immediately because finding vulnerabilities protects patients
B. Pause active testing of that API and request confirmation or expanded authorization
C. Test first as long as no destructive tools are used
D. Ask another researcher to test it so you do not violate your own authorization
Scenario 2
A hospital needs a risk-assessment method, initial SOC alert handling and a plan for clinical operations during a major disaster. Which combination best matches those purposes?
A. ISO 27002 / Tier 3 / SLA
B. ISO 27005 / Tier 1 / BCP
C. ISO 27701 / SOC Manager / NDA
D. ISO 27001 / Incident Commander / AUP
Scenario 3
An SSD containing sensitive patient records will go to an external recycler. It was encrypted, but unencrypted areas and external key copies cannot be ruled out. What should be done?
A. Delete the files and empty the recycle bin
B. Assume that deleting a key necessarily qualifies as Purge
C. Check encryption coverage and media properties, use a suitable sanitization method, and verify and record the result
D. Hand it over directly because SSD data is difficult to recover
Scenario 4
A system uses a 64-bit block cipher with a 256-bit key, processing large data volumes under the same key. What warrants further assessment first?
A. A 256-bit key means no cryptographic risk exists
B. Brute force is the only possible security problem
C. Block size, mode and data volume may introduce birthday-bound risks
D. Increasing the key to 448 bits guarantees a solution to every problem
Scenario 5

An enterprise API sends data and its SHA-256 digest, but an attacker may modify both. The service also uses HTTPS, while the client fails to validate the server certificate properly. Which improvement is most appropriate?
A. Replace SHA-256 with Base64
B. Correctly validate the TLS server identity and use authenticated integrity protection as required
C. Repeat SHA-256 ten times to resolve identity validation
D. Increase compression so attackers cannot recognize the content

The learning objective is to identify the real security goal, the mechanism used and the conditions required for its guarantees. These judgments support reasoning about further CEH questions beyond memorizing nine answers.

zh.title: 第 3 部分｜M20：從加密原理到簽章與題幹判斷

sections.heading: 第一階段｜密碼學的工作與術語

body.text: 本部分對應原始第 19–27 題，從 M20 對稱／非對稱加密到數位簽章。目標是建立可解變形題的原理，不只背 AES、RSA、DSA 或 Twofish 名稱。
銀行傳送一筆新臺幣 10 萬元交易，可能同時要求不被偷看、不被改成 100 萬元、確認來源為可信銀行，以及安全建立通訊金鑰。單一演算法不會自動完成這四件事。
1. 密碼學的四類工作

rows: 雙方如何取得共同秘密

body.text: 四類並列於「保護資訊與建立可信通訊」的密碼學主幹，不是四個必經順序；之後將各演算法放回其工作位置。
2. 六個基本術語
Transfer NT$100,000 to Account B 是銀行要傳送的原始指令。

rows: 加密後無法直接理解原內容的資料
以適當金鑰與程序還原
規定資料如何運算、轉換
控制運算的秘密值或相關材料

body.text: 演算法像保險箱鎖具機構，金鑰像鑰匙。演算法通常公開，秘密金鑰才需保密；現代密碼學不應只靠藏住演算法。
3. 從位元到密文
Bit 只有 0 或 1，8 bits 組成一 Byte；ASCII 字母 A 可表示為 01000001。加密依金鑰執行設計過的數學轉換。

rows: 例如 AES-256 加上秘密金鑰與適當程序
7F 2A 91 C0 5B ...（示意，非實際 AES 結果）

body.text: Base64 與十六進位是公開可逆的表示方式，不是秘密加密。實際密碼系統另需運作模式、初始化資料、金鑰管理與錯誤處理；只說「AES-256」不足以證明系統安全。

sections.heading: 第二階段｜對稱加密與 AES 選拔

body.text: 對應第 19、21 題。分清共享秘密、區塊長度、金鑰長度，再看 AES 選拔歷史。
1. Symmetric Encryption
Alice 用一把鑰匙鎖箱子，Bob 用同一把鑰匙開啟：Alice 加密 → 共享秘密金鑰 K → Bob 解密。AES 與 Twofish 屬這一類，通常高效率、適合大量資料；難點是雙方須先安全取得共同秘密。
2. Block Cipher 的固定單位
Cipher 是密碼演算法，Block 是資料區塊。像工廠機器每次處理 16 個小盒子，即使總數上千，單次基本單位仍為 16。128-bit 區塊 = 128 ÷ 8 = 16 bytes；不是整份檔案限 16 bytes，長資料需用適當 Mode of Operation 處理多區塊。
3. Key Size 不等於 Block Size
題目 operates on 128-bit blocks, accepts keys up to 256 bits 表示兩個參數：區塊 128 bits = 16 bytes；金鑰 256 bits = 32 bytes。NIST FIPS 197 的 AES-128／192／256 均用 128-bit 區塊，因此這組數字不能唯一識別 Twofish。
4. Stream Cipher 與 Keystream

rows: 產生金鑰串流與資料逐位元／位元組結合
正確 Nonce 與串流使用規則

body.text: Keystream 是依秘密金鑰等輸入產生的位元串流。第 19 題明確給 128-bit block，即可排除不是固定區塊演算法的 RC4。
5. Twofish 與 AES 選拔
DES 因金鑰短等問題逐漸不符需求，NIST 公開評選新對稱標準。五個決選者是並列候選，不是五步流程：

rows: 獲選，成為 AES 採用的設計

body.text: 依 NIST《Report on the Development of the AES》：Twofish 像決賽選手，Rijndael 才是冠軍。問「未獲選的決選者」可答 Twofish；問「最後獲選」是 Rijndael；只問「曾進決選」則 Twofish 與 Rijndael 都符合。
6. 第 19、21 題的預期與歧義
兩題只換排序。128-bit block 排除 RC4 與 64-bit Blowfish，剩 AES／Twofish。出題者預期「決選但未獲選」的 Twofish，所以答案 D／B；但題幹未明說「未獲選」，嚴格無法排除 AES。這是措辭不足，不是密碼學定律。
真正應記住：AES 與 Twofish 都採 128-bit 區塊、都可使用 256-bit 金鑰；Twofish 是決選者，Rijndael 是獲選設計。

sections.heading: 第三階段｜VeraCrypt 與磁碟威脅模型

body.text: 對應第 20 題 EC-Q024。難點是區分靜態儲存保護與主機已遭入侵時的防護能力。
1. Disk、Partition、File
想像 1 TB SSD 存 Windows、資料庫、照片與文件。Disk 是實際或邏輯儲存裝置，Partition 是其劃分區域，File 是其中資料；像整棟大樓、各樓層與房間文件。
2. 三種儲存加密與掛載／解鎖

rows: 整個磁碟或系統儲存範圍
實際範圍依產品與設定

body.text: 妥善加密的筆電關機後遺失，可降低拆 SSD 離線讀取資料的風險，這是 Encryption at Rest（靜態資料加密）。但登入後開檔，系統就需提供明文。Mounted Volume 指已接入檔案系統路徑；Unlocked Volume 指已有解密金鑰可用，兩者相關但不同，加密磁碟通常先解鎖才能正常存取。
3. VeraCrypt 與 Hidden Volume
VeraCrypt 可建加密容器，也支援分割區等儲存裝置加密。假設外層容器看起來有 100 GB，可在外層可用空間建立另一密碼的 Hidden Volume（隱藏磁碟區）。外層存一般加密資料，內層存希望額外隱藏的資料；這是包含關係，不是兩個先後磁碟，也不表示真實配置比例。
Plausible Deniability（合理否認性）希望在特定條件下，僅由容器外觀難以證明另有隱藏區。它不是永不發現保證：若對手反覆取得不同時間的磁碟快照，可能從變更線索推論；仍須遵循產品安全前提。官方亦要求不要把隱藏磁碟區存於使用耗損平均的裝置，例如 SSD；這個包含關係例子不是此類裝置的配置建議。
4. 為何加密不能直接阻止已入侵主機外洩？

rows: 已解鎖，攻擊者有足夠讀取權限
磁碟加密無法單獨阻止明文存取

body.text: 合法應用讀檔時，某環節必須解密；有足夠權限的攻擊者可沿相同路徑讀明文。VeraCrypt 官方也指出磁碟加密不是記憶體加密，已開啟檔案明文與必要金鑰可能在 RAM。這是威脅模型差異，不是某產品獨有問題。
Threat Model 先定義對手、能力與能接觸的資料，再評估防護。實際應變應依程序控制存取、阻止外洩並保全證據，不是在受入侵主機貿然大量加密。
5. 第 20 題：功能辨識與實務限制同時保留
選項含 BitLocker、FileVault、Rohos、VeraCrypt。BitLocker 是 Windows 磁碟加密，FileVault 是 macOS 磁碟資料保護；Rohos 也有加密儲存與隱藏分割區功能，不能只憑「隱藏」就排除。題幹整組特徵，特別是外層容器內以不同密碼建立 Hidden Volume，最指向 D. VeraCrypt。
考試辨識功能時可選 D；題幹若暗示加密已掛載磁碟就立即阻止已入侵主機讀病歷，實務結論不成立。
6. 同一 AES，不同運作模式
引擎相同可用在不同機器：AES 是核心，Mode of Operation 規定長資料或特定場景的用法。XTS-AES 常用儲存保密，AES-GCM 在正確使用下提供加密與完整性驗證。NIST SP 800-38E 明示 XTS-AES 本身不提供資料認證；不能說用了 AES 就同時保證不被偷看與竄改。

sections.heading: 第四階段｜公鑰、RSA 與 DH

body.text: 1. 對稱加密遇到的困難
對應第 22、23 題並連到 24–27。Alice、Bob 未見過面，若用 AES 傳合約，Bob 仍需正確秘密金鑰；不安全管道直接傳送可能被攔截，這是 Key Distribution Problem。
2. 公鑰與私鑰的關係
Asymmetric Cryptography 使用依演算法建立、有數學關係的 Key Pair（金鑰對）：Public Key 可公開，Private Key 須保護。對支援公鑰加密的方案，寄件者無須先與每位收件者共享同一秘密。

headers: Alice 寄機密文件給 Bob
rows: 公鑰可公開，但身分必須可信
Bob 用自己的私鑰解密
Alice 不需要 Bob 私鑰

body.text: 非對稱不等於都能加密檔案：RSA 有加密與簽章方案，DSA 主要做簽章，Diffie–Hellman 做金鑰協議。
3. RSA 的不同安全方案
RSA 取自 Rivest、Shamir、Adleman，是公鑰密碼系統；主要數學背景涉及大整數模運算與整數分解相關困難性。先理解金鑰數學關係能支援多種方案，不必先推導所有數學。
RFC 8017 分別規範這些方案，不是把公私鑰運算方向對調就能安全完成所有功能。第 23 題 P3-Q056 問非對稱加密，選項 A AES、B DES、C RSA、D Blowfish；其餘皆對稱演算法，供稿答案 C. RSA。
4. Diffie–Hellman：公開交換仍可建立秘密
DH 是 Key Agreement。安全條件成立時，雙方公開交換資訊，各自算同一秘密，並不直接傳它。顏色類比：共同公開基底，各自混入秘密顏色，交換混合結果後再用保留秘密做可交換順序的混合，得到相同結果。真正 DH 用群運算，不是物理顏料。
5. 用小數字核對 DH
以下刻意使用不安全小參數，只作數學示範。公開 p = 23、g = 5；p 是模數質數，g 是指定群的生成元或基底。mod 是取餘數，例如 29 mod 23 = 6。Alice 秘密 a = 6，Bob 秘密 b = 15。
Alice 未把 a 傳給 Bob，Bob 未把 b 傳給 Alice，卻都得到 K = 2。真實協定需要安全參數、驗證與 KDF；不能拿此玩具例子的參數保護資料。
6. 能旁聽公開值，與能替換公開值不同
公開值當然可以被攔截；安全參數與假設下，僅靠它們難以可行地算出秘密。但主動攻擊者 Eve 可替換公開值：Alice 以為對方是 Bob，Bob 以為對方是 Alice，Eve 卻分別與兩人建立不同秘密，攔截後再加密轉送。這是 MITM（中間人攻擊）。
DH 必須搭配身分驗證，才能處理這類攻擊；「建立秘密」不等於「知道正在和誰建立秘密」。
7. HTTPS 的混合式分工
以憑證驗證伺服器、使用 ECDHE 的 TLS 1.3 為例，下表依原稿概念流程保留成功與失敗分支，不當成逐封包時序。

rows: 依金鑰排程以 HKDF 導出適用流量金鑰

body.text: TLS 是保護網路通訊的協定；ECDHE 用暫時性秘密與橢圓曲線；HKDF（HMAC-based Key Derivation Function）由秘密材料導出不同用途金鑰；AEAD 同時加密並驗證完整性與指定附加資料。這是 Hybrid Cryptosystem：公鑰機制協助建鍵，高效率對稱機制保護大量資料。TLS 1.3 也支援 PSK 等配置；現行 RFC 9846 取代供稿第 3 份仍引用的 RFC 8446。
供稿答案 D. Asymmetric encryption。Disk Encryption 保護儲存，Symmetric Encryption 不會自動解決首次共享秘密，Hash Functions 不能單獨完成安全建鍵。更精確稱 Public-Key Key Establishment，包含傳送、協議或封裝，不宜全部混稱非對稱加密。

sections.heading: 第五階段｜數位簽章與驗證

body.text: 對應第 24–27 題。Encryption 防偷看，Hash 產生資料指紋，Signature 產生可由公鑰驗證的私鑰簽署證據，先分清任務。
1. Hash 與文件指紋
交易文件「付款 NT$100,000 給廠商 A」經 SHA-256 產生 256-bit Digest（Hash Value）；這是固定長度摘要，流程未提供實算值。若被改成 NT$1,000,000，通常摘要會大幅不同，稱 Avalanche Effect（雪崩效應）。Hash 不是 Encryption，沒有持金鑰解密回原文的用途；不同輸入仍可能碰撞，安全性要求難以找到可利用碰撞。
2. 文件與 Hash 一起被換掉
攻擊者改交易金額，再附自己重算的 Hash，接收者比對仍一致。這只證明文件與所附摘要相符，不能單靠未保護摘要證明來源為銀行，需適當 Signature 或 MAC（Message Authentication Code，訊息認證碼）。
