body.text: 5. 第 26 題：簽章不保證保密與可用
銀行寄出已簽交易文件，取得文件與簽章的人仍可能閱讀原文，因簽章未把文件變密文。防偷看用加密，驗來源與完整性用適當簽章；兩者都需要時，適當組合。簽章也不能保證伺服器不當機或網路不中斷。
第 26 題 P3-Q071 供稿答案 B. Integrity, Non-repudiation, and Authentication。Confidentiality、Availability、Privacy、Speed 等選項不是簽章直接提供的完整安全性質組合。

sections.heading: 第六階段｜RSA、DSA、DH、ElGamal

body.text: 對應第 24、25、27 題。RSA、DSA、DH、ElGamal 都涉及公鑰密碼學，但須用用途與具區辨力的特徵辨認。
1. 四種技術的比較

rows: 公鑰系統、整數分解相關困難、模冪
加密、簽章與特定金鑰建立方案
數位簽章、每訊息秘密 k
離散對數與隨機秘密值

body.text: RSA、DSA 與 ElGamal 都可能用模運算或模冪。只寫 modular arithmetic 不足唯一識別 RSA。
2. DSA 的每訊息秘密與公開域參數
DSA 是 Digital Signature Algorithm。傳統簽署除了永久私鑰，還需每訊息秘密 k（Per-message Secret Number，可視為此運算的 Nonce）。這份額外秘密材料若處理不當，可能暴露永久私鑰。結果為簽章二元組 (r,s)，由摘要、私鑰、k 與公開參數計算。
Public Domain Parameters 的 Domain 是數學運算環境，不是網域名稱，也不是 DNS。
3. 為何不能不安全地重用 k？
簡化核心關係：s = k^(-1) × (H(m) + x r) mod q。H(m) 是摘要，x 是私鑰，k 是該次秘密，r、s 是簽章值，q 是子群階；此處略去摘要截取等細節。
k^(-1) 是模 q 的乘法反元素，不是一般浮點除法。不同文件若不安全地用相同 k，公開簽章可能形成可解出 x 的關係。因此永久私鑰與簽章過程秘密材料都要保護，隨機數產生器亦重要。
RFC 6979 的 Deterministic DSA／ECDSA 可依私鑰與摘要確定性推導合適 k，不必每次取得新外部隨機輸入；這不同於對不同訊息意外重用不安全 k。
4. 現代標準中的 DSA
NIST FIPS 186-5 在 2023 年發布，不再核准 DSA 產生新簽章，只保留驗證標準實施日前產生的簽章。新簽章技術含 RSA、ECDSA、EdDSA。考題可依傳統 DSA 特徵作答，但新設計若受該標準約束，不能把舊式 DSA 當預設。
線索是每次新隨機值、公開群與子群模運算、公鑰驗證。傳統 DSA 最符合預期，供稿答案 C. DSA。RSA 也能簽，但此組參數與 k 更指向 DSA；DH 主要為金鑰協議。ElGamal 簽章也用一次性秘密並有共同數學特徵，原題仍有歧義，不把單一線索當定律。
計算交易 Hash、私鑰簽署、公鑰驗證不能單獨辨認 RSA，DSA 也有這個概念流程。額外線索是同一演算法家族支援加密、簽章與金鑰建立，因此供稿答案 A. RSA；NIST SP 800-56B Rev. 2 包含 RSA-based 傳送與協議方案。
多種用途必須區分具體安全方案，不表示同一組金鑰應全部兼用；FIPS 186-5 對 RSA 簽章金鑰用途有隔離要求。TLS 1.3 也已移除傳統 Static RSA Key Exchange。
7. 第 27 題 EC-Q084：公鑰目錄的信任
私鑰簽署、公鑰驗證與模冪不能唯一識別 RSA，DSA／ElGamal 類方案也部分符合；B. RSA 是供稿題庫預期。更重要的是：驗證所用公鑰真屬銀行嗎？
若攻擊者可改公鑰目錄，就能建自己的金鑰、簽假交易、以自己的公鑰冒充銀行。數學驗證可能成功，卻錯把結果當銀行授權。PKI 與可信金鑰綁定要處理這個問題。

cards.question: 為什麼 128-bit Block + 256-bit Key 不能唯一識別 Twofish？
answer: AES 也符合；需要額外區辨條件，且「AES 決選者」也包含獲選的 Rijndael。

cards.question: 全磁碟加密為何仍可能讓攻擊者讀病患資料？
answer: 磁碟已解鎖且攻擊者有權限時，可沿應用讀取路徑取得明文；靜態加密不是入侵清除。

cards.question: DH 能建秘密，為何仍有中間人風險？
answer: 若不驗證公開值的來源，對手可替換並分別與兩端建秘密。

cards.question: 單獨 SHA-256 為何不能證明交易來自銀行？
answer: 誰都能對假交易重算摘要；需可信公鑰簽章或合適認證機制與身分綁定。

cards.question: DSA 的 k 為何不能在不同訊息不安全重用？
answer: 重用可暴露足以推回私鑰的數學關係；可用安全隨機來源或適當確定性方案，並遵循現代演算法標準。

cards.question: RSA 驗證成功為何不等於真正銀行授權？
answer: 驗證公鑰可能被冒換；即使可信綁定正確，還須檢查交易權限、時效與業務規則。

body.text: 單元 1｜對稱式加密：AES 與 Twofish 到底差在哪裡？
1. 白話理解：兩個人使用同一把鑰匙
想像你與同事有一個保險箱。你把文件放進去、上鎖；同事拿到同一把鑰匙，就能開箱。
這就是 Symmetric Encryption（對稱式加密）的核心概念：
加密與解密使用相同的秘密金鑰，或能直接相互推導的秘密金鑰。
兩個人都必須保護這把鑰匙。
2. 正式定義：Block Cipher 與 Key Size
題目出現兩個數字：

items: 128-bit block：演算法每次處理 128 位元，也就是 16 bytes 的資料區塊。
256-bit key：加密使用的秘密金鑰長度為 256 位元，也就是 32 bytes。

body.text: 這兩個數字在描述完全不同的性質。

body.name: bytes
body.caption: 區塊長度與金鑰長度
body.description: 每格代表 1 byte＝8 bits。上排 16 格、下方 32 格是兩項獨立參數；AES 的 128／192／256-bit 金鑰都搭配 128-bit 區塊。

items.title: Block Size：128 bits＝16 bytes
items.body: 一次交給區塊加密演算法處理的資料份量

items.title: Key Size：256 bits＝32 bytes
items.body: 控制加密轉換的秘密金鑰長度

body.text: 為什麼要分清楚？
因為演算法可以固定一次處理 128 bits，卻允許使用不同長度的金鑰。AES 就有 AES-128、AES-192、AES-256 三種標準金鑰長度，但它們的區塊長度都固定為 128 bits。
Block Size 並不等於 Key Size，也不能單靠這兩個數字推斷演算法名稱。
3. 為什麼答案是 Twofish，不是 AES？
這題真正有區辨力的資訊，是 AES 競賽的歷史。
1990 年代，美國 NIST 為了制定取代 DES 的新加密標準，公開徵求並評估候選演算法。

body.text: 這裡要區分：

Rijndael：參加決選，最後獲選為 AES。
AES：選拔完成後的標準名稱，並不是另一個與 Rijndael 無關的演算法。

body.text: 因此，第 19 與第 21 題預期選 Twofish。
不過，題目只說「AES selection process 的 finalist」，而 Rijndael 也是 finalist。因此，若嚴格檢驗題目邏輯，應補上「但未獲選」才足以完全排除 AES 選項。目前的答案是合理的考試預期答案，不代表原題沒有歧義。

body.text: Blowfish 的設計者文件確認它使用 64-bit block；IETF 也早在 RFC 7465 禁止於 TLS 協商 RC4 cipher suites。
5. 進階：只有 AES-256，是否就能說資料很安全？
不能。
你至少還需要知道使用哪一種 Mode of Operation（運作模式），以及金鑰、初始化值與驗證機制如何管理。
例如，AES-GCM 不只提供加密，也能產生 Authentication Tag，用來驗證資料是否遭到未授權修改；但這必須建立在正確使用 nonce、金鑰等條件之上。
實務上，正確實作、金鑰管理與適當的加密模式，和演算法名稱一樣重要。
單元 2｜磁碟加密：VeraCrypt 能防止已入侵的駭客偷資料嗎？
這是本批題目中，最需要區分「題庫邏輯」與「資安事件應變」的一題。
1. 白話理解：鎖起整個房間，不代表房間內的人看不到東西
把檔案加密想成鎖住一個抽屜；把磁碟區加密想成鎖住整個房間。
但是，如果房間的門已經打開，攻擊者也已經進入房間，即使外面有很厲害的鎖，也無法阻止他讀取房間內可存取的文件。
這就是資料加密非常重要的界線：
Encryption at Rest（靜態資料加密）主要保護未解鎖的儲存資料，不能取代受入侵系統的存取控制與事件應變。
2. 三種儲存加密層次

body.text: 3. VeraCrypt 為什麼符合題目？
題目給了三項條件：
第一，要能建立 encrypted containers（加密容器）。
第二，要能加密整個分割區或磁碟區。
第三，還要能建立 hidden volumes（隱藏磁碟區）。
VeraCrypt 同時具有這些功能，其中 Hidden Volume 是最具辨識力的提示。

但需要注意：系統活動紀錄、暫存資料與不同時間點的磁碟快照，都可能洩漏隱藏磁碟區存在的線索；寫入外層磁碟區也可能破壞隱藏磁碟區。這些都是 VeraCrypt 官方文件明確提醒的限制。

5. 題目最大的問題：伺服器已遭入侵
題目說攻擊者正在外洩病患資料，分析師希望立刻加密已掛載的主要磁碟區，阻止進一步外洩。
這個因果關係不成立。
假設攻擊者已取得能讀取病患資料的系統權限：

items: 磁碟區掛載、解鎖後，應用程式與具足夠權限的使用者可以讀到解密後的資料。
攻擊者若掌握相同或更高的權限，也可能讀到資料。
此時新增磁碟加密不會自動終止攻擊者的存取能力。
在受入侵的主機上進行大型加密操作，還可能改變數位鑑識證據。

body.text: VeraCrypt 官方也明確指出，攻擊者若取得已掛載磁碟區的電腦，通常可以讀取其中的資料。

單元 3｜非對稱密碼學：兩個陌生人如何安全建立共同金鑰？
1. 白話理解：不必先把秘密鑰匙交給對方
假設你要寄一份機密文件給素未謀面的人。
使用對稱加密時，雙方需要先有一把共同的秘密金鑰。但如果你必須透過不安全的網路交付這把金鑰，就可能被攔截。
非對稱密碼學提供了不同的方法：
每個參與者可以有一組彼此對應的金鑰：

items: Public Key（公鑰）：可以公開。
Private Key（私鑰）：應由持有者秘密保管。

body.text: 某些非對稱演算法允許任何人使用接收者的公鑰加密資料，只有持有相應私鑰者才能解密。
這種設計能避免直接傳送解密所需的私鑰。
但並非所有非對稱演算法都能加密訊息；有些只能交換金鑰或產生簽章。
2. 對稱、非對稱與 Hash 是不同種類的工具

rows: 加密、簽章或金鑰建立，視演算法而定
將資料映射成固定長度摘要
訊息完整性與來源認證

body.text: Hash 有一個很重要的特性：
它不是用來將摘要「解密回原文」，而是用來計算資料的指紋。
例如，對一個 1 GB 的檔案計算 SHA-256，可以得到 256-bit 摘要。如果檔案改變，摘要通常也會改變。
但是攻擊者若能同時替換檔案與旁邊的 Hash 值，單純比較兩者就無法可靠證明原始檔案未遭惡意修改。
因此，Hash 通常要搭配 MAC 或 Digital Signature，才能建立具有金鑰保障的來源驗證。
3. Key Transport 與 Key Agreement 的差別
這是第 22 題背後真正值得理解的重點。
Key Transport（金鑰傳送／傳輸）：一方產生金鑰材料，透過保護機制交付另一方。
Key Agreement（金鑰協議）：雙方各提供部分秘密材料，透過協定算出共同秘密，不必直接傳送該共同秘密。

body.text: Diffie–Hellman 的核心數學
假設雙方事先知道公開參數 p 與 g。
Alice 選秘密值 a，Bob 選秘密值 b。
Alice 傳送：
A=g^a mod  p
Bob 傳送：
B=g^b mod  p
雙方分別計算：
K_A=B^a mod  p
K_B=A^b mod  p
由模冪運算的性質：
K_A=K_B=g^{ab} mod  p
所以兩人可以得到同一個共同秘密。
這個公式的安全性不是來自「模運算很複雜」而已，而是來自正確選擇群參數、離散對數相關問題的計算困難性，以及安全實作的其他條件。
實際上通常還要再透過 KDF 導出可使用的對稱金鑰。
4. 重大陷阱：Diffie–Hellman 本身不能防止中間人攻擊
如果 Alice 只知道自己收到某個公開值，卻不能確認那個值真的來自 Bob，攻擊者 Eve 就可能攔截與替換交換值。

body.text: Alice 以為自己在跟 Bob 通訊，Bob 也以為自己在跟 Alice 通訊，但兩人的通訊可能實際經過 Eve 解密與重新加密。
因此，DH 解決共同秘密的建立問題；憑證、數位簽章及經驗證的協定則用來解決對方是否可信的問題。
這也是為什麼 TLS 不只是單獨執行一次 DH 計算。

EC-Q053：D. Asymmetric encryption
題目希望利用非對稱密碼學，協助雙方安全分配或建立金鑰。
其他選項：

items: Disk encryption：保護儲存資料，不是用來建立通訊雙方的共同金鑰。
Symmetric encryption：用既有秘密金鑰加密效率很高，但沒有自行解決首次建立共同秘密的問題。
Hash functions：用來計算摘要，不能單靠 Hash 建立安全的雙方金鑰交換。

body.text: 更精確地說，題目應問 Asymmetric Cryptography / Public-Key Key Establishment，而不是把所有非對稱金鑰建立機制統稱為 encryption。
P3-Q056：C. RSA
四個選項中，AES、DES、Blowfish 都是對稱加密；RSA 是公鑰密碼演算法。
這題不需要背誦所有演算法，只要先分辨「單一秘密金鑰」與「公私鑰機制」，就能排除三個錯誤選項。
單元 4｜數位簽章：如何證明交易沒有被竄改？
1. 白話理解：加密信封與簽名是兩回事
假設銀行要送出一份交易確認書。
如果擔心別人偷看，就把確認書放進加密信封。
如果擔心別人偽造銀行的確認書，就需要能夠驗證來源的數位簽章。
兩者目的不同：

items: Encryption：讓未授權的人看不懂。
Digital Signature：讓驗證者能檢查訊息是否被修改，以及是否由對應私鑰簽署。

body.text: 數位簽章不是把手寫簽名照片貼上去，而是利用密碼學演算法產生一組可驗證的資料。
2. 數位簽章的實際流程

body.text: 這個流程還有一個重要前提：
接收者必須先確定用來驗證的公鑰，確實屬於他認為的簽署者。
若攻擊者能把公鑰目錄中的銀行公鑰換成自己的公鑰，他就可能以自己的私鑰簽署偽造訊息，再讓使用者拿被替換的公鑰驗證。
數學驗證可以通過，但身分結論是錯的。
這是 Public Key Infrastructure（PKI）、憑證與信任鏈的重要性。

body.text: NIST FIPS 186-5 將數位簽章的資料完整性、簽署者認證與不可否認性列為重要用途。
但在銀行交易或法律證據情境中，不能只因為 Signature 驗證成功，就推論當事人本人一定親自操作或同意該交易。
例如，私鑰可能遭竊、簽章服務可能遭到濫用，或操作人員可能根本未經授權。

body.text: 使用 k 及私鑰計算簽章的兩個部分 (r,s)。
關鍵是：如果 k 被重複使用、洩漏或產生過程有可利用的偏差，可能導致私鑰遭到推算。
這也是為什麼隨機數產生品質是數位簽章安全的重要環節。
但需要補充兩個重要事實：
第一，ElGamal 簽章也使用一次性秘密值，所以「有隨機數」不是 DSA 的唯一特徵。
第二，RFC 6979 定義了 Deterministic DSA / ECDSA，能安全地從私鑰與訊息摘要推導 k，不必每次都依賴新產生的外部隨機數。相同訊息在相同私鑰下可能產生相同簽章，因此不能說所有安全 DSA 實作都必須每次取得真正新的隨機輸入。
更重要的是，NIST FIPS 186-5 已不再核准 DSA 用來產生新的簽章，只保留既有 DSA 簽章的驗證用途。新系統在對應 NIST 標準的情境下，可考慮 RSA、ECDSA、EdDSA 等方案。
因此第 24 題：
P1-Q085：C. DSA
DSA 最吻合題目描述的群參數與傳統簽章機制。
RSA 是另一種簽章家族；DH 主要用於金鑰協議；ElGamal 在數學特徵上存在重疊，但 DSA 的特定子群參數設計使它成為較合理的預期答案。
RSA：同一種數學基礎可以支援不同密碼學服務
RSA 的基本結構有公鑰與私鑰，並使用模冪運算。
以簡化的 RSA 數學原型表示：
c=m^e mod  n
m=c^d mod  n
這展示 RSA 公私指數之間的數學對應，但這不是可以直接部署的安全加密程式。
實際應使用經過安全設計的 RSA 方案，例如：

items: RSAES-OAEP：公鑰加密。
RSASSA-PSS：數位簽章。

body.text: 這兩種方案有不同目的與編碼要求。RFC 8017 分別定義其運作方式。
至於金鑰建立，NIST SP 800-56B Rev. 2 也涵蓋以 RSA 為基礎的金鑰傳送及協議方案。因此，不能一概說 RSA 在任何情況下都與金鑰建立無關。
但這不代表一組 RSA 金鑰應當同時混用於加密、簽章及所有其他用途。實際設計須遵守金鑰用途分離、協定要求及安全生命週期管理。
5. 回到第 25 題：為什麼選 RSA？
P2-Q034：A. RSA
題目描述：

items: 對交易資料計算 Hash。
以私鑰簽署。
用公鑰驗證。
文件宣稱演算法支援加密、數位簽章及金鑰建立。

body.text: 題庫顯然想考 RSA 的多用途特性。
但前面三個步驟只是一般數位簽章流程，DSA、ECDSA 等也可以符合。最後一項描述才是試圖區分答案的條件。
嚴格而言，題目需要指定實際的簽章方案或 RSA 金鑰參數，才能明確識別；它也不應把不同 RSA-based schemes 說成單一演算法自然同時完成所有功能。
所以，A 是最符合出題意圖的答案，但題幹無法構成完整的技術鑑別。
6. 回到第 26 題：不可否認性是否絕對成立？
P3-Q071：B. Integrity, Non-repudiation, and Authentication
這是數位簽章典型考點。
A 的 Confidentiality、Availability 不是數位簽章直接提供的組合；C 的 Encryption、Privacy 混淆加密與簽章；D 的 Speed、Efficiency 不是其主要安全目標。
但必須記得：
不可否認性是有條件的證據保障，不是任何法律爭議下都不可推翻的絕對結論。
例如，HSM 金鑰保管、憑證管理、時間戳記、簽章操作紀錄及授權程序，都會影響簽章能支持何種歸屬結論。
7. 回到第 27 題：模冪運算能直接判斷是 RSA 嗎？
EC-Q084：B. RSA（考試預期答案）
這題的問題比第 25 題更明顯。
題幹提到：

items: 私鑰簽署、公鑰驗證。
公鑰保存在目錄中。
使用 Modular Exponentiation（模冪運算）。
可能遭受 Man-in-the-Middle Attack。

body.text: 然而 DSA 與 ElGamal 類型的簽章也涉及模冪運算。私鑰簽署與公鑰驗證更是一般公鑰簽章的共同性質。
所以，這些條件不足以唯一鑑定 RSA。
如果希望能夠明確判定 RSA，應提供更獨特的資訊，例如 RSA 模數 n=pq、公開指數 e，或明確的 RSA-PSS 簽章格式與方案識別。
另外，題目將中間人攻擊歸因於「演算法的金鑰結構」，也過度簡化。
真正需要檢查的是：公鑰目錄能不能被竄改？驗證者是否確實驗證公鑰與銀行身分之間的可信關係？
這才是對支付系統有直接防禦價值的問題。

sections.heading: 續篇供稿｜三、從九題提煉出的五項重要判斷

rows: AES 也可能符合，必須找額外鑑別資訊
有 AES-256 就能防止資料外洩
必須先確認磁碟是否已掛載、主機是否遭控制
非對稱加密都可以交換金鑰與簽章
需分辨各演算法及具體方案支援的功能
私鑰簽章、公開金鑰驗證就代表 RSA
DSA、ECDSA、ElGamal 簽章也有相關機制
數位簽章通過就代表本人操作
還要確認公鑰身分、私鑰保管及授權流程

sections.heading: 續篇供稿｜五、理解檢核：五道新情境題

body.text: 本階段不提供答案。請先作答並說明判斷依據。

sections.heading: 續篇供稿｜情境應用測驗

body.text: 1. 題目 1｜演算法識別
工程師發現一套加密演算法使用 128-bit block、256-bit key，並曾進入 AES 競賽最後五強。有同事立刻斷言它一定是 Twofish。這個推論是否成立？
A. 成立，只有 Twofish 符合這些條件
B. 不成立，因為只有 AES 支援這些條件
C. 證據不足，應進一步檢查演算法識別資訊
D. 應判斷為 RC4
2. 題目 2｜受入侵主機的加密防護
某醫院資料庫使用全磁碟加密，但系統目前已解鎖運作。攻擊者利用取得的系統權限持續讀取病患資料。下列哪種應對方向最合理？
A. 把磁碟金鑰從 128-bit 改為 256-bit 即可中止外洩
B. 依事件應變程序隔離威脅、保全證據並處理遭入侵的存取權限
C. 將資料移至另一個已掛載的加密容器即可
D. 只要重新計算所有檔案的 Hash 即可防止竊取
3. 題目 3｜DH 與中間人攻擊
Alice 與 Bob 使用 Diffie–Hellman 成功建立共同秘密，但沒有驗證交換的公開值是否來自對方。請說明攻擊者可能如何利用這個缺口，以及可以加入哪一類機制修補。
4. 題目 4｜數位簽章與身分驗證
一家銀行的 RSA-PSS 交易簽章通過驗證，但驗證用的公鑰來自一個可能遭竄改的公開目錄。能否立即認定交易由該銀行授權？請說明原因，並指出簽章是否能保護交易內容不被偷看。
5. 題目 5｜DSA 私鑰安全
某舊系統的 DSA 簽章服務，因隨機數產生器故障，對兩筆不同交易重複使用同一個 k。請解釋可能的安全後果，並說明依據 NIST FIPS 186-5，是否應繼續使用 DSA 產生新的簽章。
本次課程的核心能力目標，不是只記住 Twofish、VeraCrypt、RSA、DSA 等名稱，而是看到新的系統情境時，能先辨認要保護的安全性質，再推理哪種密碼學機制真正有用、哪些必要條件尚未成立。
下一步是完成上面的五道情境題；批改時應特別檢查能否區分「數學上驗證成功」與「系統安全目標確實達成」。

en.title: Part 3 | M20: encryption, signatures and question reasoning

sections.heading: Stage 1 | Cryptographic jobs and terms

body.text: This part covers supplied references 19–27, from M20 symmetric/asymmetric cryptography to signatures. The objective is reasoning that transfers to reworded questions, rather than memorizing names such as AES, RSA, DSA or Twofish.

A bank transmitting an NT$100,000 transaction may need to prevent reading, prevent alteration to NT$1,000,000, authenticate a trusted bank source and establish communication keys securely. One algorithm does not automatically accomplish all four.
1. Four cryptographic jobs

rows: AES, Twofish and RSA encryption schemes
RSA-PSS, ECDSA, EdDSA and traditional DSA

body.text: These four categories share the purpose of protecting information and enabling trusted communication. They are not four mandatory sequential stages. Place each algorithm according to its job.
2. Six foundational terms
Transfer NT$100,000 to Account B is the bank’s original instruction.

rows: Data whose original content cannot be read directly
Recover data with an appropriate key and procedure
Secret values or related material controlling the operation

body.text: An algorithm resembles the safe’s lock mechanism; a key resembles its key. Algorithms are commonly public, while secret keys need confidentiality. Modern cryptography should not depend only on concealing the algorithm.
3. From bits to ciphertext
A bit is 0 or 1, and 8 bits form a byte. ASCII A can be represented as 01000001. Encryption applies designed mathematical transformations controlled by a key.

rows: For example, AES-256 with a secret key and suitable procedure
7F 2A 91 C0 5B ... (illustrative, not an actual AES result)
The correct key and decryption procedure

body.text: Base64 and hexadecimal are publicly reversible representations, not secret encryption. Real cryptosystems also require modes, initialization data, key management and error handling. Saying “AES-256” alone does not establish system security.

sections.heading: Stage 2 | Symmetric encryption and AES selection

body.text: References 19 and 21. Distinguish shared secrets, block size and key size, then examine AES selection history.
1. Symmetric encryption

Alice locks a box with a key and Bob opens it using the same key: Alice encrypts → shared secret key K → Bob decrypts. AES and Twofish belong to this category. They are generally efficient for bulk data, but both parties must first obtain the common secret safely.
2. The fixed unit of a block cipher

Cipher means a cryptographic algorithm and block means a data unit. A factory machine handling 16 small boxes at once still uses that unit when processing thousands. A 128-bit block is 128 ÷ 8 = 16 bytes. It does not limit an entire file to 16 bytes; a suitable mode handles longer data across blocks.
3. Key size is not block size

Operates on 128-bit blocks, accepts keys up to 256 bits describes two parameters: a 128-bit/16-byte block and a 256-bit/32-byte key. AES-128, AES-192 and AES-256 in NIST FIPS 197 all retain a 128-bit block. These values therefore cannot uniquely identify Twofish.
4. Stream ciphers and keystreams

rows: Generate a keystream combined with data bits/bytes

body.text: A keystream is a bit stream generated from a secret key and related inputs. An explicit 128-bit block in reference 19 excludes RC4, which is not a fixed-block cipher.
5. Twofish and the AES selection

DES no longer met evolving needs because of issues including its short key. NIST held a public selection for a new symmetric standard. The five finalists were parallel candidates, not five process stages:

rows: Selected as the design used for AES

body.text: NIST’s Report on the Development of the AES distinguishes finalist Twofish from winner Rijndael. A nonselected finalist can be Twofish; the selected algorithm is Rijndael. Merely asking who reached the final includes both.
6. Expected answers and ambiguity in references 19 and 21

rows: A RC4, B AES, C Blowfish, D Twofish
A Blowfish, B Twofish, C RC4, D AES

body.text: The questions only reorder options. A 128-bit block excludes RC4 and 64-bit-block Blowfish, leaving AES and Twofish. The intended nonselected finalist is Twofish, giving D/B. But without an explicit “not selected” condition, AES cannot strictly be excluded. This is incomplete wording, not a cryptographic law.
Retain the actual facts: AES and Twofish both use 128-bit blocks and support 256-bit keys; Twofish was a finalist and Rijndael was selected.

sections.heading: Stage 3 | VeraCrypt and disk threat models

body.text: Reference 20, EC-Q024. Distinguish protection of stored data from protection after a running host is compromised.
1. Disk, partition and file

Imagine a 1 TB SSD holding Windows, databases, photos and documents. A disk is a physical or logical storage device, a partition is a divided region and files hold data. The analogy is a whole building, its floors and documents in rooms.
2. Three storage-encryption scopes and mounting/unlocking

rows: Use it like a disk after mounting
Actual protected regions depend on product and configuration

body.text: If a properly encrypted laptop is lost while shut down, encryption at rest can reduce the risk of reading its removed SSD offline. After login and opening a file, however, plaintext must become available. Mounted means attached to a filesystem path; unlocked means the keys needed for decryption are available. These related states are distinct; encrypted volumes generally need unlocking for ordinary access.
3. VeraCrypt and hidden volumes

VeraCrypt creates encrypted containers and supports encryption of partitions and other supported storage. An outer container appearing to hold 100 GB can contain a hidden volume in its free space under another password. Ordinary encrypted data belongs in the outer volume; additional concealed data belongs in the hidden one. This is containment, not two consecutive disks or a proportional layout.

Plausible deniability aims to make an additional hidden region difficult to demonstrate from the container’s appearance under specified conditions. It is not a guarantee of permanent concealment: repeated disk snapshots can expose change patterns. The product’s security requirements still apply. They also prohibit storing hidden volumes on wear-leveling devices such as SSDs; this containment example is not a configuration recommendation for those devices.
4. Why encryption alone does not stop exfiltration from a compromised host

rows: Unlocked, attacker has sufficient read permissions
Disk encryption alone does not stop plaintext access

body.text: An application must decrypt data somewhere to read it. An attacker with sufficient privileges may use the same access path. VeraCrypt documents that disk encryption is not memory encryption; opened-file plaintext and necessary key material may be in RAM. This is a threat-model distinction, not unique to one product.

A threat model defines the adversary, capabilities and accessible data before evaluating protection. Response should follow procedures to control access, stop exfiltration and preserve evidence rather than blindly performing bulk encryption on the compromised host.
5. Reference 20: distinguish product features and operational limits

Options include BitLocker, FileVault, Rohos and VeraCrypt. BitLocker is Windows disk encryption and FileVault protects macOS disk data. Rohos also offers encrypted storage and hidden-partition features, so “hidden” alone does not exclude it. The combined clues, particularly a hidden volume inside an outer container under a separate password, best point to D, VeraCrypt.
D is the supplied exam expectation, but any suggestion that encrypting a mounted volume immediately prevents an intruder from reading medical records is not an adequate operational conclusion.
6. The same AES, different modes

The same engine can power different machines. AES is the core cipher; its mode defines use for longer data or a particular setting. XTS-AES commonly protects storage confidentiality, while correctly used AES-GCM provides encryption and integrity verification. NIST SP 800-38E states that XTS-AES itself does not authenticate data. Using AES alone does not establish both confidentiality and tamper detection.

sections.heading: Stage 4 | Public keys, RSA and DH

body.text: 1. The distribution problem for symmetric encryption

References 22 and 23 also connect to 24–27. If Alice and Bob have never met and use AES for a contract, Bob still needs the secret key. Sending it directly through an insecure channel risks interception: the key-distribution problem.
2. The public/private key relationship

Asymmetric cryptography uses an algorithm-specific, mathematically related key pair. The public key can be shared and the private key must be protected. Public-key encryption schemes let a sender communicate without first sharing the same secret with every recipient.

headers: Alice sends Bob a confidential document
rows: It can be public but its identity must be trusted
Bob decrypts with his private key
Alice never needs Bob’s private key

body.text: Asymmetric does not mean every algorithm encrypts files: RSA has encryption and signature schemes, DSA mainly signs and Diffie–Hellman establishes keys.
3. Different RSA schemes

RSA takes its name from Rivest, Shamir and Adleman. It is a public-key cryptosystem involving large-integer modular arithmetic and hardness related to factoring. Its related keys support different schemes; understanding their roles comes before a full mathematical derivation.

RFC 8017 specifies these as separate schemes. Reversing the direction of public/private operations does not securely implement every function. Reference 23, P3-Q056, asks for an asymmetric encryption algorithm among A AES, B DES, C RSA and D Blowfish. The others are symmetric, so the supplied answer is C, RSA.
4. Diffie–Hellman: establishing a secret through public exchange

DH is key agreement. Under suitable security conditions, parties publicly exchange information and independently compute the same secret without directly sending it. A color analogy uses a public base, private colors, exchanged mixtures and a further order-independent mixing step. Actual DH uses mathematical group operations, not physical paint.
5. Check DH with small numbers

The deliberately tiny parameters below are insecure and only illustrate the mathematics. Public values are p = 23 and g = 5: p is the prime modulus, and g is the group generator or base. Mod means remainder, for example 29 mod 23 = 6. Alice’s secret is a = 6 and Bob’s is b = 15.
Alice does not send a, and Bob does not send b, yet both obtain K = 2. Real protocols require secure parameters, validation and a KDF. These toy parameters must not protect actual data.
6. Observing public values differs from replacing them

Public values can be intercepted. Under secure parameters and assumptions, observing them alone should not feasibly reveal the secret. An active Eve can instead replace them: Alice thinks she is talking to Bob, Bob thinks he is talking to Alice, while Eve establishes different secrets with each and decrypts/re-encrypts relayed traffic. This is a man-in-the-middle attack.
DH requires authentication to address that attack. Establishing a secret does not establish who shares it with you.
7. Hybrid cryptography in HTTPS
For certificate-authenticated TLS 1.3 using ECDHE, this table preserves the source’s conceptual success/failure branches, not a packet-by-packet timeline.

rows: Derive suitable traffic keys through the HKDF-based key schedule
Protect data with a scheme such as AES-GCM

body.text: TLS protects network communication; ECDHE uses ephemeral secrets and elliptic curves; HKDF, HMAC-based key derivation function, derives purpose-specific keys; AEAD encrypts and authenticates integrity and specified associated data. This hybrid cryptosystem uses public-key mechanisms for establishment and efficient symmetric mechanisms for bulk traffic. TLS 1.3 also supports configurations such as PSK. Current RFC 9846 replaces RFC 8446, which this third source still cited.
8. Reference 22, EC-Q053

The supplied answer is D, Asymmetric encryption. Disk encryption protects storage, symmetric encryption does not automatically establish an initial shared secret, and hash functions alone do not securely establish keys. Public-key key establishment is more precise and includes transport, agreement or encapsulation rather than calling all of them asymmetric encryption.

sections.heading: Stage 5 | Digital signatures and verification

body.text: References 24–27. Encryption prevents reading, hashes produce fingerprints and signatures provide private-key signing evidence verifiable with a public key. Distinguish the jobs first.
1. Hashes and document fingerprints

The transaction “Pay NT$100,000 to supplier A” produces a 256-bit SHA-256 digest, or hash value. This is a fixed-length fingerprint; no computed value was supplied. Changing it to NT$1,000,000 usually changes the digest substantially, illustrating the avalanche effect. Hashing is not encryption and has no key-based decryption purpose. Collisions still exist; security requires exploitable collisions to be difficult to find.
2. Replacing both document and digest

An attacker changes the amount and supplies a newly calculated hash. A receiver can still find a match. That proves consistency with the accompanying digest, not a bank origin. Appropriate signatures or MACs, message authentication codes, provide authentication mechanisms.
3. The conceptual signing and verification flows

rows: Apply the bank private key and signature scheme
Establish the bank public key’s trusted identity
Verify M and S with the public key and specified scheme
Invalid signature; do not rely on it
Cryptographic evidence concerning the signature and integrity
Still check transaction authorization, freshness and business rules

body.text: The reflowable HTML tables preserve the source flowcharts’ conditional branches. This is not generically encrypting a digest with a private key. RSA-PSS uses an encoding procedure and DSA/ECDSA use their own equations; the tables describe shared concepts.
4. Three properties and conditions for non-repudiation

rows: Does the signature verify under the bank’s trusted key?
Is there evidence supporting that a party signed?

body.text: NIST FIPS 186-5 supports these signature uses. Stolen private keys, a compromised signing system or flawed authorization can still cause disputes. Successful verification is not an unconditional bar to denial.

Security hardware protecting keys and performing cryptographic operations
Evidence of who acted, when and through which procedure

body.text: 5. Reference 26: signatures do not guarantee confidentiality or availability

Anyone obtaining a signed bank document and its signature may still read the original because signing does not encrypt the document. Use encryption against reading and an appropriate signature for origin/integrity evidence; combine mechanisms where both goals matter. A signature also cannot keep a server running or a network connected.

Reference 26, P3-Q071, has supplied answer B, Integrity, Non-repudiation, and Authentication. Combinations involving confidentiality, availability, privacy or speed do not describe the direct set of signature properties being asked for.

sections.heading: Stage 6 | RSA, DSA, DH and ElGamal

body.text: References 24, 25 and 27. RSA, DSA, DH and ElGamal are related to public-key cryptography but differ in purpose and distinguishing features.
1. Compare four techniques

rows: Public-key system, factoring-related hardness, modular exponentiation
Encryption, signatures and specific key-establishment schemes
Digital signature and per-message secret k
Discrete logarithms and random secret material

body.text: RSA, DSA and ElGamal can all involve modular arithmetic or exponentiation. Modular arithmetic alone does not uniquely identify RSA.
2. DSA per-message secrets and public domain parameters

DSA means digital signature algorithm. Traditional signing requires a per-message secret number k, used as a nonce in this operation, in addition to the long-term private key. Mishandling that extra secret can expose the permanent key. The resulting pair (r,s) depends on the digest, private key, k and public parameters.

rows: Prime modulus for the finite field
Prime order of the relevant subgroup

body.text: Domain in public domain parameters identifies the mathematical setting, not an Internet domain name or DNS.
3. Why is unsafe reuse of k dangerous?

A simplified core relation is s = k^(-1) × (H(m) + x r) mod q. H(m) is the digest, x the private key, k the per-message secret, r and s signature values and q the subgroup order. Details such as digest truncation are omitted here.

k^(-1) is the multiplicative inverse modulo q, not ordinary floating-point division. Unsafe reuse of k for different documents can expose relationships in public signatures that reveal x. Protect both long-term keys and signing secrets; the random-number generator also matters.

RFC 6979 describes deterministic DSA/ECDSA, deriving a suitable k from the key and digest without fresh external random input each time. That differs from accidentally reusing an unsafe k across different messages.
4. DSA in the modern standard

NIST FIPS 186-5, published in 2023, no longer approves DSA for signature generation and retains verification of signatures generated before the standard’s implementation date. Generation techniques include RSA, ECDSA and EdDSA. Recognize traditional DSA in exam scenarios without making it the default for new designs subject to that standard.
5. Reference 24, P1-Q085

Fresh random signing values, public group/subgroup parameters and public-key verification most strongly suggest traditional DSA, the supplied answer C. RSA signs too, but these parameters and k point more toward DSA; DH primarily agrees keys. ElGamal signatures also use per-message secrets and share mathematical features, so the wording retains ambiguity rather than giving a universal identification rule.
6. Reference 25, P2-Q034

Hashing a transaction, signing privately and verifying publicly do not alone identify RSA; DSA has that conceptual flow too. The additional clue is one family supporting encryption, signatures and key establishment. The supplied answer is A, RSA. NIST SP 800-56B Rev. 2 includes RSA-based transport and agreement schemes.

Different purposes require distinct secure schemes; they do not justify using one key pair for everything. FIPS 186-5 restricts reuse of RSA signing keys for other purposes. TLS 1.3 also removed traditional static RSA key exchange.
7. Reference 27, EC-Q084: trust in a public-key directory

Private signing, public verification and modular exponentiation do not uniquely identify RSA; DSA/ElGamal-related schemes share some features. B, RSA is the supplied expected answer. The more important question is whether the verification key really belongs to the bank.

An attacker controlling a directory can generate keys, sign a fake transaction and substitute their public key for the bank’s. Mathematical verification may pass while bank authorization is falsely inferred. PKI and trusted key binding address this problem.

rows: Mathematical verification succeeds under the specified public key
A trusted procedure confirms binding to the expected identity

body.text: The first does not automatically establish the second; neither replaces transaction authorization, freshness or business-rule checks.

cards.question: Why do a 128-bit block and 256-bit key not uniquely identify Twofish?

cards.question: Why can an attacker still read patient data despite full-disk encryption?
answer: An unlocked disk and sufficient privileges can expose plaintext through application access. At-rest encryption is not intrusion removal.

cards.question: Why can DH still suffer a man-in-the-middle attack?
answer: Without authenticating the source of public values, an attacker can replace them and establish separate secrets with each endpoint.

answer: The verification key may have been substituted. Even with a trusted binding, check transaction permissions, freshness and business rules.

November 10, 2026 | Questions 19–27 | An integrated concept course
Cryptography uses distinct mechanisms to address confidentiality, key establishment, authentication and data integrity. Transforming data into unreadable text is only one of these tasks.
For example, a bank transmitting transaction data may use:

items: AES: make intercepted data difficult for unauthorized parties to understand.

body.text: Unit 1 | Symmetric encryption: how do AES and Twofish differ?
References: 19. EC-Q493 and 21. P1-Q114
1. Plain-language explanation: two people share a key
You put a document in a safe and lock it. A colleague opens it using the same key.
This illustrates symmetric encryption:
Encryption and decryption use the same secret key, or secret keys directly derivable from each other.
Both people must protect that key.
2. Formal definitions: block cipher and key size
The question mentions two numbers:

items: 128-bit block: the algorithm processes 128 bits, or 16 bytes, in each block.
256-bit key: the secret encryption key contains 256 bits, or 32 bytes.

body.text: They describe different properties.

body.name: bytes
body.caption: Block size and key size
body.description: Each cell represents 1 byte = 8 bits. The 16 block cells and 32 key cells describe independent parameters; AES keys of 128, 192 or 256 bits all use 128-bit blocks.

items.title: Block size: 128 bits = 16 bytes
items.body: Amount of data processed by one block-cipher operation

items.title: Key size: 256 bits = 32 bytes
items.body: Length of the secret key controlling the transformation

body.text: Why distinguish them?
An algorithm can process a fixed 128-bit block while accepting different key lengths. AES-128, AES-192 and AES-256 have distinct standardized key lengths, but all use 128-bit blocks.
Block size and key size are different, and these numbers alone do not identify the algorithm.
3. Why is Twofish the expected answer rather than AES?
The AES competition history provides the relevant distinguishing context.
In the 1990s, NIST publicly solicited and evaluated candidates for a new encryption standard to replace DES.

body.caption: Selection of the AES standard
body.description: Arrows show historical selection stages. Twofish and Rijndael were both finalists; Rijndael was selected. Finalist status, 128-bit blocks and a 256-bit key alone do not uniquely identify Twofish.

Rijndael: a finalist that was selected as AES.
AES: the resulting standard, not another algorithm unrelated to Rijndael.

However, Rijndael was also an AES finalist. A strictly discriminating question should add “but was not selected” to rule out the AES option fully. Twofish is a reasonable intended exam answer, while the supplied description still has ambiguity.

No.
You must also identify the mode of operation and the management of keys, initialization values and authentication.
For example, AES-GCM encrypts and generates an authentication tag to help detect unauthorized changes, provided nonce and key requirements are followed correctly.
Correct implementation, key management and suitable modes matter alongside the algorithm name.

1. Plain-language explanation: a lock does not hide files from someone already inside
File encryption resembles locking a drawer; volume encryption resembles locking an entire room.
If the door is already open and an attacker is inside, a strong exterior lock does not stop them reading accessible documents.
This establishes a boundary for encryption:
Encryption at rest primarily protects locked storage data; it cannot replace access control and incident response on a compromised system.
2. Three storage-encryption scopes

Activity records, temporary data and snapshots taken at different times may reveal clues about its existence. Writing to the outer volume can also damage the hidden volume. VeraCrypt documentation warns about these limitations.

An attacker with equivalent or higher privileges may read it too.
Adding disk encryption does not automatically remove the attacker's access.

Full-disk encryption is important for a stolen laptop. If an attacker already controls a running server, the immediate priorities are unauthorized-access containment, stopping exfiltration and preserving evidence.

Unit 3 | Asymmetric cryptography: how can strangers establish shared key material?
References: 22. EC-Q053 and 23. P3-Q056; related to questions 25 and 27
1. Plain-language explanation: no need to deliver the private key first
Suppose you want to send a confidential document to someone you have never met.
Symmetric encryption requires a shared secret first. Delivering it over an insecure network may expose it to interception.
Asymmetric cryptography provides other approaches:
Each participant can possess corresponding keys:

items: Public key: may be disclosed publicly.
Private key: must be kept secret by its holder.

body.text: Some asymmetric algorithms let anyone encrypt data with a recipient's public key, while only the corresponding private-key holder can decrypt it.
This avoids sending the decryption private key directly.
Not every asymmetric algorithm encrypts messages; some are designed for key agreement or signatures.
2. Symmetric encryption, asymmetric cryptography and hashes are different tools

rows: Encryption, signatures or key establishment, depending on the algorithm
Map data to a fixed-length digest

body.text: A key property of a hash is:
It computes a data fingerprint; it is not intended to “decrypt” a digest back into its original input.
SHA-256 maps a 1 GB file to a 256-bit digest. Changing the file normally changes the digest.
If an attacker can replace both the file and the adjacent digest, a match does not reliably establish that the original file escaped malicious modification.
A hash therefore commonly works with a MAC or digital signature to provide keyed origin authentication.
3. Key transport versus key agreement
This is the concept behind question 22 worth understanding.
Key transport: one party generates key material and securely delivers it to another through a protective mechanism.
Key agreement: both parties contribute secret material and derive a shared secret through the protocol without directly transmitting that shared secret.

body.name: keymethods
body.caption: Two ways to establish shared keys
body.description: Read each column downward; the columns are parallel comparisons. Authentication, secure schemes and a KDF remain necessary; RSA transport here does not imply static RSA exchange in TLS 1.3.

items.body: Alice generates secret key K

items.title: Protect using a public key

items.title: Recover using a private key

items.body: Alice and Bob each choose secret values

body.text: The core Diffie–Hellman mathematics
Suppose both parties know public parameters p and g.
Alice chooses secret a; Bob chooses secret b.
Alice sends:
A = g^a mod p
Bob sends:
B = g^b mod p
They calculate independently:
K_A = B^a mod p
K_B = A^b mod p
Modular exponentiation gives:
K_A = K_B = g^(ab) mod p
Both therefore derive the same shared secret.

Security requires appropriately selected group parameters, the computational difficulty of discrete-logarithm-related problems and other implementation conditions; it does not follow merely from modular arithmetic looking complicated.
A KDF normally derives usable symmetric keys from the shared secret.
4. A major limitation: unauthenticated Diffie–Hellman does not prevent a man-in-the-middle attack
If Alice cannot establish that a received public value came from Bob, Eve can intercept and replace the exchanged values.
The result can be:

body.text: Alice and Bob may each believe they communicate directly, while Eve decrypts and re-encrypts traffic between them.
DH establishes shared secret material; certificates, signatures and authenticated protocols establish trust in the peer.
TLS therefore involves more than a standalone DH calculation.
5. How does modern HTTPS combine the mechanisms?
Consider a typical TLS 1.3 connection using a server certificate and ECDHE:

6. Return to questions 22 and 23
EC-Q053: D. Asymmetric encryption
The question intends public-key cryptography to help distribute or establish keys securely.
Other options:

items: Disk encryption protects stored data; it does not establish a communications secret between peers.

body.text: More precisely, the question should ask about asymmetric cryptography or public-key key establishment instead of calling every asymmetric establishment mechanism “encryption.”
P3-Q056: C. RSA
AES, DES and Blowfish are symmetric ciphers; RSA is a public-key cryptographic algorithm.
Distinguishing a shared secret from a public/private-key mechanism eliminates the three unsuitable options without memorizing every algorithm detail.
Unit 4 | Digital signatures: how can transaction modification be detected?
1. Plain-language explanation: encrypted envelopes and signatures have different purposes
Suppose a bank sends a transaction confirmation.
To prevent unauthorized reading, put it in an encrypted envelope.
To detect a forged bank confirmation, use a signature whose origin can be verified.
Their purposes differ:

items: Encryption prevents unauthorized understanding of the content.
A digital signature lets a verifier check changes and the relationship to a corresponding private key.

2. The signing and verification process

body.text: An important precondition remains:
The recipient must establish that the verification public key belongs to the intended signer.
If an attacker replaces the bank's public key in a directory, they can sign forged messages with their own private key and have users verify them with the substituted key.
The mathematical check can succeed while the identity conclusion is wrong.
This explains the role of PKI, certificates and trust chains.

For banking transactions or legal evidence, successful signature verification alone does not establish that the individual personally operated the signer or authorized that transaction.
The private key may have been stolen, the signing service abused or the operator unauthorized.
4. Distinguish RSA, DSA, Diffie–Hellman and ElGamal

body.text: RSA and DSA are both asymmetric, but DSA is not an RSA encryption mode.
DSA: protect the per-signature secret k
The main clues in question 24 are:
Each signature uses a new secret value and modular arithmetic within a subgroup defined by public group parameters.
Traditional DSA signing relies on:

items: Public parameters p, q, g

body.text: The private key and k are used to compute the signature components (r, s).
Reusing, exposing or producing exploitable bias in k may permit private-key recovery.
This makes high-quality per-signature secret generation important to signature security.
Two additional facts matter:
First, ElGamal signatures also use a per-signature secret. Randomness alone does not uniquely identify DSA.

Second, RFC 6979 defines deterministic DSA/ECDSA, deriving k securely from the private key and message digest rather than requiring fresh external randomness for each signature. The same message and key may produce the same signature, so secure DSA implementations do not universally require a newly obtained random input each time.

NIST FIPS 186-5 no longer approves DSA for generating new signatures, retaining verification of existing DSA signatures. Systems governed by that standard may instead consider RSA, ECDSA or EdDSA for new signing designs.
Return to question 24:
P1-Q085: C. DSA
DSA most closely fits the described group parameters and traditional signing mechanism.
RSA is another signature family, while DH primarily performs key agreement. ElGamal overlaps mathematically, but DSA's specific subgroup parameters make it the more reasonable intended answer.
RSA: one mathematical foundation supports distinct cryptographic services
RSA uses corresponding public/private keys and modular exponentiation.
A simplified mathematical prototype is:
c = m^e mod n
m = c^d mod n
These equations illustrate the relation between RSA exponents; they are not deployable secure encryption code.
Use standardized secure schemes, for example:

items: RSAES-OAEP: public-key encryption.
RSASSA-PSS: digital signatures.

body.text: The schemes have different purposes and encoding requirements. RFC 8017 defines them separately.
NIST SP 800-56B Rev. 2 also covers RSA-based key-transport and agreement schemes. It is therefore inaccurate to say RSA can never participate in key establishment.
This does not mean the same RSA key should be mixed across encryption, signing and every other purpose. Designs must follow key-use separation, protocol requirements and lifecycle controls.
5. Return to question 25: why is RSA expected?
P2-Q034: A. RSA
The question describes:

items: Hash the transaction data.
Sign with a private key.
Verify with a public key.
Documentation claims support for encryption, signatures and key establishment.

body.text: The intended distinguishing theme is RSA's range of uses.
The first three steps are generic to signatures and may also fit DSA or ECDSA. The final description attempts to distinguish the answer.

A technically precise identification would specify the signing scheme or RSA parameters. It should also distinguish separate RSA-based schemes rather than implying one algorithm automatically performs every service together.
A best matches the apparent exam intent, while the question description is insufficient for definitive technical identification.
6. Return to question 26: is non-repudiation absolute?
P3-Q071: B. Integrity, Non-repudiation, and Authentication
This is a conventional signature-properties question.

A includes confidentiality and availability, which signatures do not directly provide as a combination. C confuses encryption and privacy with signatures. D lists speed and efficiency rather than the principal security goals.
Retain this condition:
Non-repudiation is conditional evidence, not an unchallengeable conclusion in every legal dispute.
HSM custody, certificate management, timestamps, signing logs and authorization procedures all affect the attribution a signature supports.
7. Return to question 27: does modular exponentiation identify RSA?
EC-Q084: B. RSA (intended exam answer)
The ambiguity is even greater here than in question 25.
The description mentions:

items: Private-key signing and public-key verification.
Public keys kept in a directory.
Modular exponentiation.
Possible man-in-the-middle attacks.

body.text: DSA and ElGamal signatures also involve modular exponentiation. Private-key signing and public-key verification are shared properties of public-key signature mechanisms.
These conditions therefore do not uniquely identify RSA.
More specific evidence would include an RSA modulus n = pq, public exponent e or an explicit RSA-PSS scheme identifier and signature format.
Attributing a man-in-the-middle risk simply to “the algorithm's key structure” also oversimplifies the issue.
Ask whether the public-key directory can be modified and whether the verifier authenticates the binding between the key and the bank.
Those questions directly inform defenses for a payment system.

sections.heading: Continuation | 3. Five important judgments from these nine references

rows: A 128-bit block and 256-bit key identify Twofish
AES can fit too; seek additional discriminating evidence
Check whether storage is mounted and the host compromised
Every asymmetric mechanism exchanges keys and signs
Distinguish supported services of each algorithm and scheme
Private-key signing with public-key verification identifies RSA
DSA, ECDSA and ElGamal signatures share related mechanisms
A valid signature proves personal operation
Check identity binding, private-key custody and authorization

body.text: Use this reasoning process for exam questions:

body.name: reasoning
body.caption: Reason from question evidence to the best answer
body.description: Arrows show the reasoning process. Yes leads to the best answer; no records the intended exam answer and ambiguity while retaining the insufficiency of the evidence.

items.title: Read the question
items.body: Read the complete prompt and options

items.title: Identify the main security objective
items.body: Confidentiality, integrity, identity or key establishment

items.title: Classify the mechanism
items.body: Encryption, key establishment, hash or signature

items.title: Find discriminating technical conditions
items.body: Check schemes, parameters, uses and assumptions

items.title: Eliminate incompatible options
items.body: Explain each exclusion

items.title: Enough evidence for a unique identification?
items.body: Check whether other mechanisms also fit

items.title: Select the best answer
items.body: Conclude when the evidence suffices

items.title: Record the intended answer and ambiguity
items.body: Retain limits when evidence is insufficient

body.text: This approach remains useful when the scenario or option order changes; a keyword-to-letter shortcut does not preserve the reasoning.

Suggested spaced-review schedule
Start with these intervals, then adjust to actual performance:

rows: Mix AES, RSA, DSA and DH
Check long-term retention and retest weaknesses

body.text: These are usable starting intervals, not a universal forgetting-curve formula. Research supports spacing and practice testing, while optimal intervals vary with retention goals and individual performance.
Use these performance distinctions:

items: Correct with a sound explanation: extend the next review interval.
Correct by guessing or incomplete reasoning: treat as unfinished learning and retain a short interval.
Incorrect or confused: revisit the reasoning, retest the next day and add a varied question.

body.text: Prioritize explaining without seeing the answer over rereading everything each day.

sections.heading: Continuation | 5. Understanding check: five new scenarios

body.text: Answers are intentionally withheld here. Attempt the questions and explain your reasoning first.

sections.heading: Continuation | Scenario application questions

body.text: 1. Question 1 | Identifying an algorithm
An engineer sees a cipher with 128-bit blocks, a 256-bit key and a place among the five AES finalists. A colleague immediately claims it must be Twofish. Is that inference justified?
A. Yes; only Twofish fits these conditions
B. No; only AES supports these conditions
C. Evidence is insufficient; inspect further algorithm identifiers
D. It must be RC4
2. Question 2 | Encryption on a compromised host

A hospital database uses full-disk encryption, but the system is unlocked and running. An attacker with system permissions continues reading patient data. Which response direction is most appropriate?
A. Change the disk key from 128 to 256 bits to stop disclosure immediately
B. Follow response procedures to isolate the threat, preserve evidence and address compromised access
C. Move the data to another mounted encrypted container
D. Recompute all file hashes to prevent theft
3. Question 3 | DH and man-in-the-middle attacks

Alice and Bob derive a shared secret with Diffie–Hellman without authenticating the exchanged public values. Explain how an attacker could exploit this gap and the type of mechanism that can address it.
4. Question 4 | Signatures and identity

A bank transaction's RSA-PSS signature verifies, but the public key came from a potentially modified public directory. Does this immediately establish authorization by the bank? Explain why, and whether the signature protects the transaction from unauthorized reading.
5. Question 5 | DSA private-key safety

A legacy DSA service reuses the same k for two different transactions because its random generator fails. Explain the possible consequences and whether FIPS 186-5 permits continued generation of new DSA signatures.

The objective is to recognize the intended security property in a new scenario, reason about which mechanism contributes and identify unmet conditions, rather than memorizing the names Twofish, VeraCrypt, RSA or DSA alone.
The next learning step is to attempt the five scenarios. Review should distinguish mathematical verification from achievement of the system's security goals.
